Dear AFA member,
With the rapid advancement of generative AI tools and their increasing use in finance research, fundamental questions are emerging about how research will be conducted and assessed going forward. Perspectives vary widely. Some emphasize the pace of technological progress and the possibility that AI could play an increasingly central role in the research process. Others are more cautious and view AI primarily as a tool for mostly well-defined tasks. A more realistic view likely lies between these positions. The research process involves elements such as taste, judgment, values, and intuition, which are not supposed to be delegated to machines. At the same time, the growing capabilities of AI tools suggest that they can play a meaningful and productive role if used thoughtfully. Finally, value tends to accrue to what is relatively scarce, and our systems for evaluating research should adapt to shifts in the relative scarcity of different inputs to and outputs from the research process.
In this context, the profession would benefit from more systematic evidence on what AI systems can produce in a research setting. A clearer understanding of this frontier helps guide the responsible use of these tools and clarify the nature of scholarly contribution. Against this backdrop, we invite submissions to a special session at the 2027 AFA Annual Meeting aimed at showcasing and evaluating the capabilities of AI in finance research, and based on that evidence, reflecting on appropriate norms for their use and the unique aspects of human contribution. Our objective is not to frame the question in terms of replacement, but rather to better understand where AI tools/agents are most effective within the research process and how they can be combined with human insight to enhance research outcomes.
We invite submissions that are predominantly generated by AI. Authors should submit entirely new projects in which AI systems play a systematic role beyond modular, tool-like functions such as variable construction or analytical assistance. We are particularly interested in work where AI contributes across multiple stages of the research process, with limited human involvement. Authors are required to document their initial inputs, data access, model configuration, and full workflow. Submissions will be evaluated by human reviewers using standard academic criteria, including the novelty and importance of the research question, the incremental contribution to the literature, and the quality of execution. In addition, this session will place specific emphasis on the extent to which the research process is carried out by AI systems, with limited human intervention.
From the submission pool, four papers will be selected for presentation in the special session based on both the research contribution and the design and effectiveness of AI use in the workflow. The expectation is not zero human involvement after the initial prompt, but the highest possible research quality per unit of human expertise and effort. In addition, all high-quality submissions will be included in an AFA 2027 online collection to provide a broad view of current AI capabilities across multiple dimensions.
Human discussants will be explicitly tasked with assessing both scientific merit and the nature of human labor embodied in each paper. They will also articulate what AI-generated finance research lacks relative to the profession’s current standards of originality and excellence. These discussions are intended to inform a broader conversation about how evaluation standards should evolve in response to ongoing technological advances.
The organizers will not use non-public information from the submission and review process for their own research. This initiative is intended as a public forum rather than a setting for data collection.
 
The ground rules for paper submissions are as follows:
•	There is no submission fee.
•	Papers can be on any topic appropriate to a top journal in finance.
•	No humans perform any work on the project, other than the named authors.
•	Each author can only submit one paper; and each author can be listed on at most three submissions.
•	The investigation of a paper should begin on or after June 1, 2026 with an initial prompt provided to an LLM or AI agent. The submission deadline is August 31, 2026.
•	All conversations with AI, including the initial prompt, must be documented and submitted along with the final paper. 
•	Humans are allowed to make direct contributions to the project outside of prompts to the AI, but these contributions should also be documented.
•	The ideal form of documentation is (1) a text of all conversations with AI, (2) a time log of human activity, and (3) a report on the fraction of project lines (code, writing, and documentation) that were contributed by humans as opposed to AI.
 
These rules intentionally leave authors wide latitude in how to structure the workflow, and in which tasks the humans adopt given their constrained time. Indeed, this variation is exactly the object of the exploration. The ideal paper is not one with no human involvement, but with maximal quality per unit of human effort.
Submission can be made through the AFA website starting in early June: https://afajof.org/ 
 
Organizers:
Itay Goldstein (Wharton School)
Wei Jiang (Goizueta Business School; Session Chair)
Robert Novy-Marx (Simon Graduate School of Business)
William Mann (Goizueta Business School)

Your instinct on the workflow split is right, and it maps well to the AFA requirements. Here's my honest assessment:

**Cowork vs Chat**

Use both, but for distinct phases:
- **Cowork** is right for the structured, file-producing work: literature review documents, hypothesis write-ups, paper drafts, and maintaining the documentation trail the AFA requires (conversation logs, time logs, code fraction reports). Files persist, are organized, and you can share them.
- **Chat** for quick iterative thinking/brainstorming where you don't need a saved output.
- **Claude Code** for the empirical pipeline: data ingestion (on-chain APIs — DeFiLlama, Glassnode, CoinGecko), computing λ, VFree, SoV/MoE, NVT/G across a panel of assets, running predictive regressions/portfolio sorts.

**Proposed Workflow for this Paper**

The natural empirical question from your framework: *Does quadrant positioning (SoV/MoE × NVT/G) predict future crypto returns?* This is novel, grounded in theory you've already developed, and testable with public on-chain data.

Phase 1 — **Literature** (Cowork): Map QTM crypto papers, NVT literature, DeFi TVL studies, find the gap your framework fills.

Phase 2 — **Theory + Hypotheses** (Cowork): Formalize testable predictions from the quadrant model.

Phase 3 — **Data + Empirics** (Claude Code): Pull on-chain data, compute your metrics, run panel regressions / portfolio sorts across quadrants.

Phase 4 — **Paper** (Cowork): Write up results, produce LaTeX or Word draft.

Phase 5 — **Documentation** (Cowork): Compile the required AI conversation logs, time log, and code fraction report for AFA submission.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-10T16:22:25.864Z

Yes, GitHub is actually a **better fit** for this project, for a few reasons specific to the AFA requirements:

**Why GitHub wins here:**

The AFA requires you to document your workflow, time log, and what fraction of the project was human vs AI. Git does this automatically — every commit has a timestamp, an author, and a diff showing exactly what changed. This is essentially a built-in audit trail, which is exactly what the organizers are asking for.

It also pairs naturally with Claude Code for the empirical work. Claude Code operates natively in git repos — it commits as it goes, so the history will clearly show AI-generated code vs your edits.

**Suggested repo structure:**

```
AFA_2027_QTM_Crypto/
├── literature/
├── hypotheses/
├── data/              ← small/processed files; raw data stays on Drive
├── code/
├── paper/             ← LaTeX or markdown
└── documentation/
    ├── ai_conversations/   ← paste/export chat logs here
    ├── time_log.md         ← running log of human hours
    └── workflow_notes.md
```

**Practical split:** use GitHub for everything (code, paper, docs, conversation logs), and Google Drive only for large raw data files that are too big for git.

One thing to decide: **public or private repo?** Private makes sense during development, then you can make it public at submission time to demonstrate transparency. 

Want me to help set up the repo structure and create the initial documentation templates (time_log.md, workflow_notes.md)?

This is a rich theoretical question. Let me share my initial synthesis, then search for the specific literature to ground it.

**My read on the theoretical landscape:**

Your λ → MOAT argument has both rational and behavioral channels, but I think the **rational channel is stronger and more defensible for an academic paper**. Here's the logic chain:

The most natural grounding is a combination of **convenience yield** and **monetary search theory**, not pure seigniorage (though seigniorage plays a supporting role).

**Convenience Yield channel:** When rational agents lock tokens, they're paying for the right to participate in the network's future utility — governance, DeFi collateral, security staking rewards. This is exactly the convenience yield in commodity finance: you pay a premium to *hold* rather than have a forward contract. High λ signals that many rational agents expect the *future convenience yield* to be high. The analogy to USD is direct — people hold dollars not just to transact but because dollar-denominated assets are uniquely liquid globally (Krishnamurthy & Vissing-Jorgensen 2012 on Treasury convenience yield is the cleanest reference here).

**The MOAT / coordination equilibrium:** The self-reinforcing part — where high λ creates the very moat it's signaling — maps directly onto Kiyotaki-Wright monetary search models. In those models, an asset becomes "money" through a coordination equilibrium: I hold it because I expect others to accept it. High λ is a public signal of that coordination. It's rational to lock *because others are locking*, and collectively this reduces circulating supply and increases the scarcity premium.

**Seigniorage:** This is real but secondary. In PoS networks, stakers capture new issuance (block rewards) — that's literal seigniorage. But the more interesting connection is **Klein (1974) on competitive currency supply** and Hayek's currency competition framework — a currency that people *want to hold* rather than spend commands a seigniorage premium precisely because holders are subsidizing its monetary premium.

**Rational vs. behavioral:** The MOAT interpretation is fundamentally rational (agents locking have a credible signal of long-term value expectations), but there's a behavioral *amplifier* — prospect theory and loss aversion make early holders extremely reluctant to sell at a loss, which mechanically keeps λ high in down markets and potentially signals survivorship. Worth acknowledging but not leading with it.

Here's the synthesis of the theoretical landscape based on what I found. This is strong — there's a clear literature path to ground your framework.

---

**The Theoretical Foundation: Four Interconnected Pillars**

**1. Monetary Search Theory (Kiyotaki-Wright, 1993) — The coordination foundation**

This is your deepest theoretical anchor. In Kiyotaki-Wright, money emerges as a coordination equilibrium: an asset becomes valuable *because* rational agents expect others to accept it. High λ is the blockchain-observable, public signal of exactly this coordination. Unlike traditional money where you can't observe who is "holding for the long term," λ is on-chain and verifiable. This makes your framework a testable extension of monetary search theory — something the original models couldn't do empirically.

**2. Convenience Yield (Sockin-Xiong 2020, Bitcoin convenience yield PMC paper) — The rational holding motive**

Sockin & Xiong (NBER w26816) model crypto tokens as platform membership where price reflects the *convenience yield from transaction surplus*. Crucially, they show token price appreciation equals total cost of capital minus the marginal user's convenience yield. High λ signals that agents expect *future* convenience yield to be high — they're paying a premium to lock in membership before adoption accelerates. This is your direct link to why USD as reserve currency commands a premium: dollar holders capture convenience yield (global liquidity, safe haven, collateral acceptability) just as high-λ crypto holders capture platform convenience yield (DeFi collateral, governance, staking rewards).

**3. Tokenomics / Adoption Dynamics (Cong, Li & Wang 2021, *Review of Financial Studies*) — The S-curve and the MOAT**

This is probably your most important citation. Cong et al. develop a full dynamic model showing that token price and platform adoption create a *self-reinforcing S-curve* — slow start, volatile middle, tapering at maturity. The intertemporal feedback between adoption and price is exactly your MOAT mechanism. High λ is a leading indicator that rational agents believe the network is approaching the steep part of the S-curve. The paper explicitly models heterogeneous agents optimizing over holding vs. transacting, which maps cleanly to your SoV/MoE decomposition.

**4. Seigniorage and Staking (Cong & He NBER w33640 "The Tokenomics of Staking", Blockchain@Polytechnique 2022) — The rational commitment device**

There's a very recent paper by Cong & He directly on staking tokenomics. The Polytechnique paper on seigniorage vs. transaction fees is also directly relevant. The key theoretical point: rational agents stake only when expected staking yield + price appreciation > opportunity cost of locking. High λ is therefore a revealed-preference signal that a large fraction of the network has positive NPV expectations. This is pure rational expectations — no behavioral story needed.

---

**On Rational Expectations vs. Behavioral**

Your instinct that this has a rational foundation is correct, and you can defend it cleanly. The behavioral amplifier (loss aversion keeping λ high in downturns via locked positions) is real but secondary and worth a footnote. The primary channel — Cong et al.'s intertemporal feedback, Sockin-Xiong's convenience yield optimization, Cong-He's staking NPV — is all rational.

---

**On Seigniorage vs. Convenience Yield as Primary Grounding**

I'd recommend **convenience yield as your primary theoretical frame** with seigniorage as a secondary mechanism, for this reason: convenience yield is a cleaner, more elegant analogy to your SoV/MoE split. Holders of USD derive convenience yield (not just seigniorage) — that's why foreigners hold dollars even at near-zero yields. Staking rewards are the crypto analog of seigniorage but the *reason* people stake is to capture the growing convenience yield of a dominant network. This maps directly to your quadrant framework: Star assets (high SoV, low NVT/G) are assets where rational agents are paying for future convenience yield that the market hasn't priced yet.

The **reserve currency analog** (Jiang et al. NBER w32454 "Exorbitant Privilege: A Safe-Asset View") is particularly elegant for your paper — just as USD holders subsidize US borrowing in exchange for a safety/convenience premium, high-λ crypto holders subsidize network security (PoS validation) and receive the "platform premium" in return.

---

**The Gap Your Paper Fills**

None of these papers: (1) decompose MC into SoV and MoE using an observable λ, (2) use SoV/MoE as a cross-sectional predictor of returns, or (3) connect this to an investment positioning framework with empirical tests. Cong et al. (2021) is closest but focuses on adoption dynamics, not investment signals. That's your contribution.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-10T17:15:24.016Z

This is exactly the right theoretical instinct, and it leads to an important extension of your framework. The distinction you're drawing maps to several rich literatures.

**The Coins vs. Tokens Problem is Real and Under-theorized**

For coins, your framework works cleanly: staking = network security provision + slashing risk + illiquidity cost = credible, costly commitment. Cong & He cover this directly.

For governance tokens like UNI, you've identified something more nuanced. The literature actually gives you three distinct categories of token holders, not two:

**Type 1 — Pure Speculative Buyer:** Buys UNI for price appreciation, no staking, no voting. This is *neither* a strong SoV nor MoE signal — it's speculative inventory. The QTM framework doesn't assign these holders a clean role.

**Type 2 — Passive Staker (locked, not voting):** Capital commitment signal only. Reduces circulating supply (contributes to λ) but zero governance voice. Moderate conviction.

**Type 3 — Active Governor (staked + votes):** Costly signal — gas fees, time, reputational risk from voting on bad proposals. This is where the MOAT signal is strongest.

The empirical DAO governance literature I found confirms this directly: a paper in *Distributed Ledger Technologies* (2024) finds that **proposal passage increases DAO token returns by 4.7%** and a **one standard deviation increase in voting participation amplifies this by 2.2%**. That is direct empirical evidence that your conjecture holds.

---

**The Edmans-Manso "Governance Through Exit and Voice" Framework**

Edmans & Manso (2011, *Review of Financial Studies*) is your theoretical anchor here. In corporate governance, blockholders govern through two channels: **Exit** (sell shares, depress price, discipline management) and **Voice** (intervene directly, propose changes). Applied to governance tokens:

- Exit = selling UNI → no MOAT signal, potentially anti-signal
- Voice = actively voting on governance proposals → MOAT signal
- Loyalty (Hirschman's third channel) = delegating to trusted representatives → moderate signal

The Uniswap-specific evidence from the DAO search confirms a further refinement: **delegation in DAOs is reputation-based** — delegates with successful proposal track records attract more delegations. This is a Spence (1973) signaling equilibrium: active governors develop reputations, reputation attracts more stake, more stake → more governance power → stronger MOAT.

---

**The TVL ≠ PQ Problem for Governance Tokens**

You've identified a real theoretical gap. For UNI *pre-fee switch*, PQ in the QTM sense was not Uniswap's TVL — it was the **governance rights over that TVL**. The Coin Metrics analysis of the UNI fee switch confirms this: after the fee switch, UNI shifted from pure governance to direct value accrual, making PQ = protocol revenue. Pre-switch the QTM link was indirect.

This suggests a refinement: for governance tokens, your framework may need a **triple decomposition** rather than dual:

**MC = MC_MoE + MC_SoV + MC_GV**

Where MC_GV is the governance value component — the option value over protocol direction, analogous to voting rights premium in corporate finance (Nenova 2003, Doidge 2004 on dual-class share voting premiums). High active governance participation inflates MC_GV, and this is the component your λ measure should capture for tokens.

---

**Empirical Design Implication**

For coins: λ = staked / circulating supply (clean, on-chain)

For governance tokens, you'd want a **composite λ**:

λ_token = α × (governance staked / circulating) + β × (voting participation rate in last N proposals)

The β weight captures the active governance signal your intuition identified. This is measurable on-chain for all major governance tokens — Uniswap, AAVE, Compound, MakerDAO all have public governance data.

---

**The Gap this Opens in the Literature**

None of the existing papers — not Cong-Li-Wang, not Sockin-Xiong, not Cong-He — make this coins vs. tokens distinction explicit in a valuation context. The DAO governance literature studies participation but doesn't connect it to QTM-style valuation. This is a clean contribution.

Want me to save this theoretical discussion to `02_hypotheses/` and start drafting the formal hypothesis section? I'd suggest structuring it as: H1 (coins/staking → returns), H2 (governance tokens: active vs. passive λ), H3 (quadrant framework predicts cross-sectional returns).

- [Blockholders and Corporate Governance — Edmans (NBER w19573)](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w19573/w19573.pdf)

**1. Introduction**

*Para 3 — Introducing λ and V_Free:* A fraction λ of supply is locked/staked and economically inert — it doesn't circulate. V_Free is the velocity of only the free-circulating supply. *Para 4 — Theoretical foundation for coins:* Coins are currencies of their native blockchain economies. Three complementary theories ground the SoV premium: (i) **monetary search theory** (Kiyotaki-Wright) — coins emerge as coordination equilibria where high λ is a public signal of that coordination; (ii) **convenience yield** (Sockin-Xiong, Krishnamurthy-Vissing-Jorgensen analog) — holders earn a non-pecuniary return from network membership, security provision, and liquidity access; (iii) **seigniorage** (Cong-He) — stakers capture new issuance, making λ a revealed-preference signal of positive NPV expectations. *Para 5 — Tokens are different — the MOAT signal:* Governance and utility tokens are currencies of their protocol economies (Cong-Li-Wang). These are all substantive and correct. Let me address each before revising, so we're aligned:

**Issue 1** — You're right. Cong-Li-Wang explicitly model platform adoption and transactional demand — they are *not* doing DCF. I'll remove them from the opening criticism and reframe: the DCF critique targets a strand of the literature (early token valuation papers, some practitioner work), and Cong-Li-Wang are actually *on our side* of the argument.

**Issue 2 & 3** — These are connected and your framing is exactly right. I'll define SoV and MoE explicitly before invoking convenience yield: MoE value = value justified by *current* transactional activity (MC_MoE = PQ/V_free); SoV value = the premium agents pay today by forgoing current exchange utility in anticipation of *future* value appreciation from network growth, adoption, and expanding utility. Then convenience yield follows naturally: agents accept lower returns on coins for the same reason Treasury holders accept lower yields — network membership has non-pecuniary value above the transactional use. That forward-looking premium IS MC_SoV.

**Issue 4** — Replace "speculative conviction" throughout with "fundamental conviction" — conviction grounded in network effects, utility growth, and adoption expectations, not irrational speculation.

**Issue 5** — Better framing: in PoS networks, newly minted tokens (inflation) are distributed to stakers — this is seigniorage in the classical sense (value transferred from non-stakers to stakers via dilution). Staking reveals that the agent believes seigniorage income plus expected appreciation exceeds the opportunity cost of locking capital. That's the positive-NPV revealed preference.

**Issue 6** — Agreed. I'll be explicit: staked governance tokens are illiquid (cannot be sold while locked). Choosing to incur that illiquidity cost is a costly Spence signal — unlike passive holding, it cannot be faked cheaply. The signal content is therefore revealed preference for future appreciation, not income-seeking.

**Issue 7** — You're right, the quadrant logic is off. Correct mapping:
- **AVOID**: High NVT/G + Low SoV/MoE — expensive relative to growth *and* low conviction. The true avoid.
- **OVERVALUED/WATCH**: High NVT/G + High SoV/MoE — expensive but believers are locking up. Not necessarily bad, but priced for perfection.
- **STAR/MOAT**: Low NVT/G + High SoV/MoE — cheap relative to growth, high conviction. Best quadrant.
- **GARP**: Low NVT/G + Low SoV/MoE — utility-driven value, low premium.

**Issue 8** — Fix email, remove duplicate sentence, add Fisher (1911) citation.

## Empirical Design — My Thoughts

### λ Measurement

**For coins**, I'd recommend three measures tested separately:

- **λ₁ (staked/total)** — staked supply / total circulating supply from Glassnode/Staking Rewards. This is the cleanest theoretical measure — explicit, on-chain coordination commitment. This should be the primary measure.
- **λ₂ (dormant/total)** — supply unmoved for ≥1 year / total supply ("HODL waves" from Glassnode). Captures conviction hodlers who signal by not transacting, not just those who formally stake. Broader than λ₁.
- **λ₃ (TVL/total)** — total value locked in DeFi contracts / total circulating supply. Directly observable from DeFiLlama but blends economic activity (TVL as PQ) with supply lockup. Use as robustness only.

Primary measure: **λ₁**. Report λ₂ and λ₃ in robustness.

**For tokens**, two measures:

- **λ₁ (governance staked/total)** — tokens staked in governance contracts / total circulating. Captures illiquidity commitment, the costly signal.
- **λ₂ (voting-weighted)** — λ₁ × (% of staked tokens that actually voted in last governance cycle). This weights for active conviction vs. passive parking. Captures the Spence signal more precisely.

Primary measure: **λ₁**. λ₂ tested as an enhancement.

The regression method I mentioned earlier was one way to create a composite: run a predictive regression of future returns on λ₁ and λ₂ jointly and let the data assign weights. The issue is that it requires a training window and risks overfitting. Better approach: test λ₁ and λ₂ separately, report both.

---

### NVT/G — Your Levelized Approach

Your instinct is right and I like it. Here's a clean implementation:

For each asset at time *t*, project TXN forward 10 years using estimated growth rate *g* (trailing 3-year CAGR of TXN), terminal growth *g_term* = 3%, discount at CAPM rate *r_e* (estimated from market beta × equity premium):

PQ* = Σ(TXN_t × (1+g)^s / (1+r_e)^s, s=1 to 10) + TV/(1+r_e)^10

where TV = TXN_10 × (1+g_term)/(r_e − g_term)

Then NVT_fundamental = MC / PQ*. No division by *g* needed — growth is already embedded in PQ*.

This is defensible and novel. I'd also test the simple version (NVT/current TXN growth rate) as a robustness check, since PQ* introduces CAPM parameter uncertainty.

---

### Asset Universe

On L1 chains — partially correct. L2s (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) post transaction data to Ethereum for security but are distinct protocol economies with their own tokens. The key distinction is:

- **Coins sample**: L1 PoS chains with native staking — ETH, SOL, AVAX, BNB, ATOM, ADA, and any others with ≥12 months of staking data. Exclude L2s (their security is rented from ETH, not independent monetary coordination).
- **Token sample**: DeFi governance tokens regardless of chain — UNI, AAVE, COMP, CRV, GMX, LDO, MKR, SNX, BAL, etc. These are protocol economies, chain-agnostic.

For survivorship bias: CoinGecko's API includes delisted assets. DeFiLlama also has defunct protocol data. I'd set a minimum threshold (e.g., ≥6 months of data, ≥$10M average market cap) to include meaningful assets while avoiding micro-tokens with no data integrity.

---

### Cross-Sectional Classification — Relative or Absolute?

Your question about how to define "high" vs. "low" is crucial. My recommendation:

**Analyze coins and tokens separately** — the signal content of λ differs fundamentally between the two. A combined sample would conflate monetary coordination signals with moat signals.

Within each sample, **classify by within-group median** at each rebalancing date (monthly or quarterly). This is standard in the cross-sectional return prediction literature (Fama-MacBeth). You're not saying λ=0.4 is always "high" — you're saying it's high relative to the cross-section at that point in time.

For tokens, grouping by protocol type makes theoretical sense and avoids apples-to-oranges comparison. Suggested groups: DEXes, lending protocols, liquid staking, infrastructure/oracles. However, within-group sample sizes will be small. I'd suggest running the full token sample first (with protocol-type fixed effects as a control), then showing robustness within groups as a supplemental test. Compare lending protocols to lending protocols, DEXes to DEXes.

---

### Portfolio Construction

Long-only Stars vs. long-only everything else is clean for practitioner audiences. For academic credibility I'd recommend:

1. **Long Stars / Short Avoids** — Fama-French style. Equal-weighted within each quadrant. Rebalance monthly. This is the cleanest test of the cross-sectional prediction.
2. **Report separately for coins and tokens** — do not pool.
3. **Factor-adjusted returns** — regress the long-short portfolio return on a 3-factor model: market (BTC return), size (small vs. large cap crypto), and momentum (past 3-month return). Alpha = the unexplained return attributable to the quadrant signal.
4. **Sharpe ratios** — report for Stars-only, Avoids-only, long-short, and the benchmark (equal-weighted all assets in sample).

One thing to think about: the Stars portfolio will naturally be concentrated in high-λ assets during bull markets (when staking is high). You'll need to check whether the alpha survives after controlling for the market cycle. A BTC-beta control should handle most of this.

---

**My suggested next session:** formalize the three hypotheses, then design the data pipeline in Claude Code. The hypotheses are straightforward from this discussion — want me to draft them now, or commit this first and pick up from there?

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-12T21:08:19.427Z

**On PMT/levelized and NVT/G:**

Yes, exactly right. PQ* is the PMT equivalent — the constant annual TXN that has the same PV as the projected stream:

PQ* = PV(TXN stream) / annuity_factor(r_e, n)

where PV(TXN stream) discounts 10 years of projected growth + terminal value, and annuity_factor = (1 − (1+r_e)^−n) / r_e. This is precisely the Excel PMT logic.

And yes — since growth is already embedded in PQ*, dividing again by G would double-count. So the primary measure is simply NVT_fundamental = MC / PQ*, no separate G adjustment. The simple NVT/G (current TXN, trailing growth rate) works well as robustness precisely because it's a cruder version of the same idea.

**On L2 as separate category:**

Good call. L2 tokens (ARB, OP, STRK, etc.) sit between coins and tokens — their chains run consensus but settle security to Ethereum. Treat them as a distinct group: L2 governance tokens. Their λ signal is governance conviction on a rollup protocol, not independent monetary coordination. Keeps the signal interpretation clean.

**On expanded DeFi categories:**

Suggested groupings:

- DEXes (UNI, CRV, BAL, RAY)
- Lending (AAVE, COMP, MKR)
- Liquid staking (LDO, RPL)
- Perpetuals/Derivatives (GMX, DYDX, SNX, HYPE if classified as token)
- Prediction markets (REP/Augur, GNO/Gnosis — small but conceptually interesting)
- Infrastructure/Oracles (LINK, GRT)
- L2 governance (ARB, OP, STRK)

Prediction markets are worth including — Polymarket itself runs on USDC so no native token, but the category has enough assets to test. If sample sizes within groups are too small (<10 assets), merge into an "Other DeFi" bucket.

**On blockchain agnostic vs. chain-specific:**

Blockchain-agnostic is the right primary approach. The QTM signal we're testing is about protocol economy conviction, not about which chain it runs on. A DEX λ signal should predict returns whether it's Raydium on Solana or Uniswap on Ethereum — if it doesn't, that's an interesting finding in itself.

Practical approach: run full sample with chain fixed effects (ETH ecosystem, SOL ecosystem, own-chain) as controls. Then within-chain as robustness. Blockchain-agnostic also gives you more power given small within-chain sample sizes.

**On HYPE — coin or token:**

HYPE is a coin by our definition. Hyperliquid is a full L1 with its own consensus (HyperBFT), and HYPE is the native asset used for staking and network validation on HyperEVM. The fact that it originated as a perp DEX doesn't change its monetary role — ETH also has a specific use case (gas) but is undeniably a coin. Classification rule: if the asset is staked to validate an independent consensus mechanism, it's a coin. If it governs a smart contract protocol on someone else's chain, it's a token. HYPE is a coin; GMX (on Arbitrum) is a token.

Worth noting this as a judgment call in the paper since HYPE is borderline — it's a young L1 where the chain and the protocol are tightly coupled. Good robustness test: reclassify HYPE as a token and see if results change.

Ready for hypotheses whenever you are.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-12T21:18:21.725Z

Sharp observation. Let me think through this carefully.

**λ has a clear theoretical channel.** Agents lock supply because of rational expectations about future convenience yield growth and network coordination. High λ is a forward-looking signal — it reveals what a large fraction of rational agents *believe* about the network's future. The return prediction follows directly: if those beliefs are correct on average, high-λ assets should earn higher returns as the expected convenience yield materializes into adoption and price appreciation.

**NVT/G does not have an equivalent structural theory.** The honest answer is that low NVT/G predicting higher returns is essentially a valuation mean-reversion argument — cheap assets relative to fundamental activity tend to appreciate. That logic comes from Cong-Li-Wang's adoption dynamics model implicitly (token prices mean-revert to adoption equilibrium), but it's the same logic as low P/E predicting equity returns. It's empirically robust across asset classes but not theoretically novel or specific to crypto.

**This actually clarifies the paper's architecture.**

The core theoretical contribution is entirely about λ. NVT/G is not a parallel theoretical signal — it answers a different, conditioning question: *is the λ signal already priced in?*

Think of it this way: high λ is a bullish signal about future conviction and adoption. But if NVT/G is also high, the market has *already* priced in that conviction. You're paying a premium for a signal everyone can see. The excess return has been arbitraged away. Conversely, when NVT/G is low, the market has *not* yet priced in the conviction signal — that's where the alpha lives.

So the real structure is:

**H1 (primary):** Higher λ/(1−λ) predicts higher future returns — the conviction/coordination signal. This is theoretically grounded in convenience yield, monetary search, and governance moat theory.

**H2 (the quadrant thesis):** The predictive power of λ is strongest when NVT/G is low — i.e., when fundamental conviction is present *and* it is not yet reflected in price. This is the interaction hypothesis, and it's your main empirical contribution. Stars (high λ, low NVT/G) are assets where the signal is present and unpriced.

**H3 (portfolio test):** A long Stars / short Avoids portfolio generates positive factor-adjusted alpha.

NVT/G on its own becomes a control variable and a conditioning device rather than a standalone predictor with its own theory. This is actually a stronger paper — one clean theoretical story (λ signals conviction, which predicts returns) with one empirical insight (the signal is only investable when not already priced in via NVT/G).

Does this restructuring match your intuition about the framework?

NVT/fundamental has no independent novel theory of its own (it's essentially value/P-E-style mean reversion) — instead it functions as a CONDITIONING variable that indicates whether the λ conviction signal is already priced in.    - **Coins vs. tokens distinction**: Coins (ETH, SOL, HYPE) = native assets of independent-consensus L1 chains; PQ = on-chain tx volume; λ = staked/total. Tokens (UNI, AAVE, GMX, ARB) = governance/utility tokens of protocol economies (chain-agnostic or L2); PQ = protocol throughput; λ = governance staked (+ voting-weighted variant).
   - **L2 as a distinct asset category**: L2 governance tokens (ARB, OP, STRK) are neither pure coins nor ordinary DeFi tokens — distinct bucket since their chains derive security from Ethereum but still have independent governance economies.
   - **HYPE classification rule**: an asset is a "coin" if it is staked to validate its own independent consensus mechanism (HYPE on HyperEVM's HyperBFT ⇒ coin); it is a "token" if it governs a smart-contract protocol on someone else's chain (GMX on Arbitrum ⇒ token). Flagged as a borderline case warranting a robustness reclassification test.
   - **Blockchain-agnostic empirical design**: primary tests pool DeFi tokens regardless of underlying chain (with chain fixed effects as controls); within-chain analysis is a robustness check only.
   - **DeFi protocol categories** (expanded per user request): DEXes, Lending, Liquid staking, Perpetuals/Derivatives, Prediction markets, Infrastructure/Oracles, L2 governance.
   - **Cross-sectional classification approach**: within-group median split at each rebalancing date (Fama-MacBeth style), coins and tokens analyzed strictly separately (never pooled, due to differing λ signal content).
   - **Portfolio construction**: long Stars / short Avoid, equal-weighted, monthly rebalancing, factor-adjusted alpha (market/BTC, size, momentum 3-factor model), Sharpe ratios reported for Stars-only, Avoids-only, long-short, and benchmark; reported separately for coins and tokens.

You caught a real gap. Let me show you exactly where it breaks, then the actual trick, then a simpler honest fix.

The individual threshold condition is fine on its own: agent $i$ stakes iff $s_t + c_{i,t+1} \geq \varphi_i$. That's just an optimal-stopping rule for one agent, no issue. The problem is the next step. To go from "agent $i$ stakes iff her own private $c_{i,t+1}$ clears her own $\varphi_i$ net of $s_t$" to "$\lambda_t = F(s_t + \bar c_{t+1})$," I silently swapped agent $i$'s own private $c_{i,t+1}$ for the population *average* $\bar c_{t+1}$ inside $F$. That substitution isn't free. If every agent has her own private $c_{i,t+1}$, the true aggregate is

$$\lambda_t = \Pr_i\big(\varphi_i \leq s_t + c_{i,t+1}\big),$$

which depends on the *joint* cross-sectional distribution of $(\varphi_i, c_{i,t+1})$, not on $F$ evaluated at the average. Writing $F(s_t+\bar c_{t+1})$ only works if $c_{i,t+1}$ is literally the same number for every agent — but then it isn't private information at all, which defeats the point of the model.

Here's the trick that actually repairs this, and it's the standard device for exactly this situation (it's what Grossman-Stiglitz 1980 and the continuum-of-agents monetary search models like Kiyotaki-Wright both lean on). Posit a single common, currently-unobserved future state $\theta_{t+1}$ — the network's "true" future convenience-yield trajectory. Each agent gets a noisy private signal of it, $x_i = \theta_{t+1} + \varepsilon_i$, with $\varepsilon_i$ idiosyncratic, mean-zero, independent across agents and of $\theta$. Each agent also has her own idiosyncratic liquidity cost $\varphi_i$, independent of everything else. Agent $i$ stakes iff $s_t + x_i \geq \varphi_i$. Aggregating over a *continuum* of agents, a law of large numbers applies to the idiosyncratic shocks $\varepsilon_i$ and $\varphi_i$: the population fraction crossing threshold converges, with no sampling error, to

$$\lambda_t = G(\theta_{t+1} + s_t),$$

where $G$ is a fixed increasing function (the convolution of $F_\varphi$ with the noise distribution of $\varepsilon$). The idiosyncratic noise cancels in aggregate, leaving $\lambda_t$ as a clean, deterministic, increasing function of the one thing common to everyone — the true state $\theta_{t+1}$ — even though no individual agent, and no outside observer, knows $\theta_{t+1}$ for certain. That's the actual mechanism: it's not "$\lambda$ is the CDF of the average belief," it's "idiosyncratic noise washes out in a continuum, so the aggregate statistic is a monotone transform of the true common fundamental." Price doesn't already reflect $\theta_{t+1}$ because inverting $\lambda_t$ back out requires knowing $G$, $s_t$, and the underlying noise distributions — exactly the costly extraction problem Grossman-Stiglitz formalize. Since $r_{t+1}$ moves with $\theta_{t+1}$ as it becomes public, and $\lambda_t$ is monotone in $\theta_{t+1}$, $\text{Cov}(r_{t+1},\lambda_t)>0$ falls out because both are increasing functions of the same $\theta_{t+1}$.

That machinery does work, but it's exactly the heavy apparatus we agreed to avoid when we picked light formalization over a full structural model. So I think your instinct is right, and the cleaner fix is yours: drop the closed-form $F(s_t+\bar c_{t+1})$ entirely. Keep the individual threshold condition — it's genuinely doing work, since it's what explains *why* a higher private belief about future convenience yield makes an agent more likely to stake. Then, instead of deriving the aggregation, state directly (with a one-line citation, not a derivation) that the aggregate staking ratio inherits the same monotonicity — more high-conviction beliefs in the holder base means more agents cross their threshold, means higher $\lambda_t$ — and posit $\lambda_t$ as a partially-revealing aggregate signal in the Grossman-Stiglitz sense: informative of dispersed private beliefs, but not fully impounded into price because extracting it is costly. Proposition 1 ($\text{Cov}(r_{t+1},\lambda_t)>0$) then follows as a stated consequence of that assumption, clearly flagged as an assumption rather than a derived result.

(For comparison, 2.2 doesn't have this problem — because beliefs there are binary, $q_i\in\{q_H,q_L\}$, the separating equilibrium makes $\lambda_t$ exactly equal to the population share of high-belief holders, no averaging trick required.)

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-19T17:08:26.397Z

Good question, and the mechanics turn out to vary a lot across real protocols — which exposes a problem in our current λ definition. Let me walk through what's actually going on.

There are three distinct things protocols call "staking" a governance token, and they have very different economics.

**Vote-escrow (ve) locking** — Curve's veCRV is the canonical example, also Balancer's veBAL and newer ve(3,3) designs like Aerodrome. Here you lock CRV for a chosen duration, up to four years, in exchange for non-transferable veCRV. What's in it for the agent is concrete and pecuniary: voting power over which liquidity pools receive CRV emissions (which protocols then bribe for — the "Curve Wars"), plus a 50% share of trading fees. Crucially, governance power scales with *both* amount and lock duration, so the illiquidity is a real, continuously-variable cost the agent chooses to bear, and longer locks are a stronger signal. This is the case that actually matches the κ/illiquidity-cost Spence model I wrote in 2.2.

**Yield-bearing staking with no lock requirement** — GMX is the cleanest example. Staking GMX pays a direct share of protocol fee revenue (reportedly around 27-30% of trading, liquidation, and borrowing fees, paid in ETH or AVAX), and governance voting rights attach to simply *holding* GMX, not to staking specifically. So GMX staking isn't really a governance-conviction signal at all — it's closer to our coin model, an $s_t$-style direct yield agents capture for bearing an unstaking cooldown, not an illiquidity-driven costly signal. (Worth flagging: GMX's DAO voted in March 2026 to pause direct staking distributions and redirect to treasury buybacks instead — a reminder that these mechanisms are not static and our data pull needs to handle regime changes within a token's own history.)

**Pure snapshot/balance voting, no staking at all** — this is Uniswap, Compound, and Aave's base governance layer. Voting power equals token balance at a snapshot block; voting itself happens off-chain via gasless signature (Snapshot). There is no lock, no staking contract, nothing to forgo. An agent votes by simply holding and signing — full liquidity preserved.

That third category is the actual problem. UNI, COMP, and AAVE are explicitly in our planned token universe, and for them "governance staked / circulating supply" — our current λ definition — isn't a small number, it's *undefined*. There's no staking action to measure. So before we even get to data construction, the theory itself needs a category our 2.2 model doesn't currently cover.

Your holding-period instinct is the right fix, and it's not even a new idea for us — it's literally already in our λ toolkit. Back in the empirical design brainstorm, we listed "supply unmoved ≥1 year / circulating (HODL waves)" as a robustness measure for *coins*. The same logic applies directly to no-lock tokens: an agent who holds through volatility without selling has forgone the option to exit, which is a real (if softer) cost under Hirschman's exit/voice framing we already cite in 2.2 — just without a discrete lock mechanism. So holding duration isn't a workaround, it's the natural λ measure for exactly the protocols where staking doesn't exist.

I'd propose resolving this with a protocol-conditional λ definition, the same pattern we used for the coin/token and L1/L2 classification rules: for ve-style or yield-staking protocols (CRV, BAL, GMX, etc.), λ = locked-or-staked / circulating, as planned. For no-lock, snapshot-only protocols (UNI, COMP, AAVE), λ = share of supply held/unmoved beyond some threshold (e.g., ≥6 or ≥12 months) — your holding-period idea, promoted from robustness check to primary measure for this subgroup. Separately, active voting participation (tokens that actually voted in a proposal over the trailing period ÷ circulating supply) becomes a second, complementary "voice" measure that applies universally regardless of mechanism — this is what tests the incremental-power claim in H1b's second sentence, just generalized from "voting-weighted staking" to "active voting" so it works whether or not a lock exists.

If you're comfortable with that three-way split, the next step is updating 2.2's language slightly — right now it leans entirely on illiquidity/κ as the cost, but the real driver should be framed as costly engagement or forgone exit optionality, of which locking is the strongest (but not only) form. Want me to make that adjustment to 2.2, or hold off until we're further along and revisit it together with the Section 4 data-construction writeup?

A random walk in t is a time-series statement about one quantity; it has no agents, no cross-section, and by itself gives no λ_t formula at all. So it doesn't replace θ, it just removes the thing that produces an aggregation result, leaving you to bolt the cross-sectional argument back on anyway.

Here's the unified Section 2.1, replacing both old 2.1 and 2.2:

---

**2.1 The Locking Decision**

Consider a continuum of agents, indexed by $i \in [0,1]$, who hold the native asset of a self-contained digital economy at date $t$---the coin of an L1 network, or the governance token of a DeFi protocol---and choose whether to lock it for one period (stake) or hold it freely circulating. Locking pays a current, publicly observed benefit $b_t \geq 0$: for proof-of-stake coins, newly issued seigniorage distributed to validators \citep{cong2024staking}; for governance tokens, a direct fee or yield share where the protocol distributes revenue to stakers, and $b_t=0$ for protocols with no such revenue share. Locking also pays a convenience yield realized at $t+1$, the non-pecuniary benefit of network or protocol membership emphasized by \citet{sockin2020model}: validation rights, governance access, and anticipated future transactional or economic capability. We decompose agent $i$'s convenience yield into a common component $\theta_{t+1}$---the asset's true future growth trajectory, unobserved at $t$, whether that trajectory is network adoption for a blockchain or product and competitive position for a protocol---and an idiosyncratic, mean-zero noise term $\varepsilon_i$ reflecting agent $i$'s imperfect private read on that trajectory: $c_{i,t+1}=\theta_{t+1}+\varepsilon_i$, with $\varepsilon_i$ i.i.d. across agents and independent of $\theta_{t+1}$. Locking also imposes a private cost $\varphi_i$, i.i.d. across agents and independent of $(\theta_{t+1},\varepsilon_i)$: the agent's own value of the liquidity and flexibility foregone. Agent $i$ locks if and only if

$b_t+\theta_{t+1}+\varepsilon_i \geq \varphi_i \iff \eta_i \leq b_t+\theta_{t+1}$, where $\eta_i \equiv \varphi_i-\varepsilon_i$.

Because $\eta_i$ is i.i.d. across the continuum with fixed CDF $H$, the strong law of large numbers implies the realized locking ratio converges almost surely to $\lambda_t = H(b_t+\theta_{t+1})$ — a deterministic, strictly increasing function of the asset's true future growth trajectory, given the publicly observed benefit $b_t$. Idiosyncratic noise washes out; what survives is the cross-sectional average of private information about $\theta_{t+1}$. This is the sense in which $\lambda_t$ is a publicly verifiable signal of the holder base's aggregate conviction — consistent with the monetary search-theoretic view of $\lambda$ as a coordination signal for coins \citep{kiyotaki1993search,lagos2005unified} and with the costly-signaling view of $\lambda$ for governance tokens \citep{spence1973job}, since locking is in both cases a costly action whose credibility rests on the same threshold condition. The model nests both institutional cases: only $b_t$ and the composition of $\varphi_i$ differ between coins and governance tokens.

That $\lambda_t$ aggregates private information about $\theta_{t+1}$ does not imply $\theta_{t+1}$ is already priced at $t$: recovering it from $\lambda_t$ requires netting out $b_t$ and inverting $H$, which requires knowing the population distribution of costs and signal noise — not common knowledge. As in \citet{grossman1980impossibility}, costly information acquisition prevents full impoundment at $t$, so realized returns are higher for higher $\lambda_t$. This partial-revelation step is the model's one substantive assumption.

**Proposition 1.** $\mathrm{Cov}(r_{t+1},\lambda_t)>0$ for both coins and governance tokens.

For L1 coins, $b_t$ is the seigniorage rate and $\varphi_i$ is the idiosyncratic value of transactional flexibility foregone.

**Hypothesis 1a (Coins).** [unchanged]

For governance tokens, $\varphi_i = \ell+\kappa_i$, where $\ell\geq0$ is a common lock-induced illiquidity cost (vote-escrow protocols like Curve, Balancer: $\ell>0$, scaling with lock duration) and $\kappa_i\geq0$ is idiosyncratic engagement cost (no-lock protocols like Uniswap, Compound: $\ell=0$, $\kappa_i$ alone sustains the threshold) — exercising *voice* rather than *exit* \citep{hirschman1970exit,edmans2011governance}. The observable action differs by mechanism, so we treat $\lambda_t$ as an empirical index over whichever channels are observable — staking/locking, holding duration, voting engagement — with construction deferred to Section~\ref{sec:data}.

**Hypothesis 1b (Governance Tokens).** [unchanged]

The voting-weighted extension: active voting requires $\psi_i>0$ beyond locking alone, so voting requires $\eta_i+\psi_i\leq b_t+\theta_{t+1}$, a strictly tighter threshold — voters are a more selected, higher-conviction subset.

Both good catches.

On L1: that restriction is a leftover, and it doesn't survive contact with your own asset universe — Section 3's planned categories already include L2 coins/token groups, so a theory that only covers L1 leaves L2 assets with no hypothesis at all. The deeper issue is that "L1 vs. L2" is the wrong cut for this model anyway. What actually matters for whether an asset belongs in the coin bucket (Hyp 1a) vs. the token bucket (Hyp 1b) is functional, not architectural: does locking it earn a security-staking benefit $b_t$ (seigniorage), or not? Some L2 native assets have validator/sequencer staking with issuance rewards — those are coins in this model's sense, full stop, regardless of layer. Others are pure governance with no staking-for-security role — those are tokens, same as UNI or COMP. Whether any specific L2 token falls into one bucket or the other is exactly the kind of classification call you've already decided to defer to Section 3, not something the theory should hard-code by naming "L1."

Fix: drop "L1" everywhere in 2.1, replace "the coin of an L1 network" with "the native coin of a blockchain network," and add a short clause: the coin/token distinction is defined by whether $b_t>0$ (a security-staking benefit exists), not by network layer, with concrete classification of L1 vs. L2 assets left to Section 3.

On the index: yes, $\lambda_t$ is asset-specific, and you're right to flag it — but careful, the letter $i$ is already taken by agents inside the model, so the asset index needs to be something else, say $j$. The reason it's fine to suppress $j$ through most of the derivation is that the agent-level threshold logic ($\eta_i \leq b_t+\theta_{t+1}$) is identical for any asset you plug in — nothing in that derivation depends on which asset $j$ you're holding fixed, so writing it once "for a given asset" and suppressing $j$ is standard, not sloppy. Where it stops being fine is Proposition 1 itself: as written, "$\mathrm{Cov}(r_{t+1},\lambda_t)>0$" is ambiguous about whether that's a time-series statement (one asset, varying $t$) or the cross-sectional statement the hypotheses actually need (many assets, same $t$). It has to be the latter — H1a/H1b are explicitly cross-sectional ("assets with higher $\lambda/(1-\lambda)$ in month $t$...") — so the proposition should say so: $\mathrm{Cov}_j(r_{j,t+1},\lambda_{j,t})>0$, covariance taken across the cross-section of assets $j$ at a given date.

One thing worth a one-line flag while we're here: that cross-sectional comparison only cleanly reflects conviction if $H$ and $b_t$ are roughly comparable across the assets being compared — otherwise two assets could differ in $\lambda$ just because they have different cost structures, not different $\theta$. Your hypotheses already guard against this by controlling for protocol category, size, and momentum, so it's not a gap, just worth one sentence acknowledging it explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-19T20:08:11.412Z

Good catch — the slash makes it read as a ratio of two named things, not "NVT, but with a redefined denominator." Best fix is to drop the slash and use an adjective before NVT instead. A few options:

**Levelized NVT** — matches language the paper already uses to describe $PQ^*$ ("levelized present value," "levelized annual equivalent," the PMT analogy). Needs no new explanation since the construction paragraph already uses this word.

**Normalized NVT** — echoes "normalized earnings," a standard valuation concept (smoothing a noisy current-period number into a more durable estimate). Most recognizable to a general finance audience, even before it's formally defined.

**Permanent NVT** — riffs on Friedman's permanent-income framing: $PQ^*$ is the asset's expected long-run throughput rather than its current, possibly-transitory throughput. Fits the paper's monetary-theory register (Fisher, search theory) nicely, but is a slightly more academic flourish.

I'd lean toward **Levelized NVT** since it's already baked into your existing vocabulary and requires zero extra setup, with Normalized as a close second if you want something more immediately legible to referees skimming the abstract. Which do you want? (Once picked, the subscript $\text{NVT}_f$ should probably change too — e.g., $\text{NVT}_L$ — happy to fold that in wherever you land.)

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-19T20:10:00.224Z

Growth-levelized is the better fit. "Normalized" is vague about mechanism — it could mean almost any rescaling (z-score, deflate, smooth). "Levelized" names the actual operation in the construction: the PMT/annuity step that converts a growing, discounted transaction stream into a flat annual equivalent. "Growth-" then flags the other distinguishing feature — that $g$ and $g_\infty$ are baked into the projection before it's levelized. Together they describe exactly what $PQ^*$ does: project growth, discount, then flatten into a level equivalent.

"Growth-normalized" risks a different misread too — readers familiar with PEG ratios (P/E divided by growth rate) might assume you're just dividing by $g$, which understates the DCF/annuity machinery actually being used.

I'd go with **Growth-Levelized NVT**, subscript $\text{NVT}_{GL}$ (or keep $\text{NVT}_g$ if you want something terser in-line). Want me to fold this into `main.tex` now, or keep discussing data/measurement first and batch the edit later?

(PowerShell will say "cannot find path" for whichever one doesn't exist — that's fine, ignore it.) Then retry your git command.

Both files are written and committed locally (`e8f93be`). Key calls made in the spec, beyond your four answers:

The "minimum capital" floor is a point-in-time rank screen (top 250 by market cap each month, adjustable), not a fixed dollar amount — crypto's total market cap grew too much from 2015–2026 for any fixed number to work across the whole sample. Once an asset qualifies, it stays in the panel permanently, even through failure, which solves the survivorship-bias problem directly. I also generalized "Etherscan" to chain-appropriate explorers plus Snapshot/Tally/Boardroom for off-chain DAO votes, since many major DAOs don't vote on-chain.

On "why just 2021" — that was a feasibility default, not a claim 2015 data is unusable. The spec now starts August 2015 (Ethereum genesis) and requires a year-by-year coverage report, since pre-2020 governance/voting data will be thin (and ETH itself only became stakeable around the 2022 Merge — flagged as a worked example of the landmines Claude Code should expect and document).

`DATA_DECISIONS_LOG.md` is the append-only file the pipeline session should use to record every proxy substitution or judgment call, per your "we may have to improvise" framing — feeds both Section 3's eventual prose and the AFA documentation trail.

Push from your machine when ready. Bibliography sanity check (task #22) is still parked.

The "thin" comment wasn't about market cap — every asset in the universe already passed the top‑250‑at‑least‑once rule (that's a market‑cap‑based gate, already applied uniformly). "Thin" meant something different and orthogonal: how many *months* that specific asset persists in the panel. Among the 874 'other'/ambiguous names, a lot are one‑ or two‑month pump‑and‑dump blips that technically crossed the top‑250 once and then vanished — reviewing those by hand is wasted effort since they barely affect a regression either way. An asset present for 60 months near the top of its class is the one worth getting right. So the proposed filter is a persistence count (months observed), not a size/rank filter — a second-stage triage on top of the already-fixed universe rule, not a change to it.

On meme coins and NFTs: meme coins (DOGE, SHIB, PEPE, etc.) are explicitly called out in the Phase 0 report as already landing in the 'other' bucket, alongside oracle/exchange/wrapped tokens — they have no staking mechanism (not "coin" under the $b_t$ framework) and no governance mechanism (not "token" either), so they don't fit your theory's classification and are excluded from H1a/H1b/H3 by construction. They do still count toward the top-250 ranking, which is correct — a meme coin occupying a real top-250 slot is genuine market structure, the same logic already applied to stablecoins. NFTs are very likely absent entirely, since the CoinMarketCap fungible-token listings endpoint Claude Code used doesn't track NFT collections at all (that's a separate CMC product) — but that should be explicitly confirmed rather than assumed, since nothing in this pipeline is supposed to rely on an unverified assumption.

On the 2x2 quadrant matrix: this is a different categorization than coin/token. Coin vs. token determines which hypothesis bucket an asset belongs to (H1a vs H1b) and which subsample it's reported in. The quadrant axes for H3 are two separate continuous variables — $\lambda/(1-\lambda)$ and Growth-Levelized NVT — each split at its cross-sectional median into high/low, crossed into four cells (Star = high-$\lambda$/low-NVT, Avoid = low-$\lambda$/high-NVT). The open design question is whether those medians should be computed separately within coins and within tokens each month, or pooled across both combined — coins and governance tokens could have structurally different staking-ratio distributions for reasons unrelated to conviction (e.g., PoS security-staking norms vs. DeFi vote-escrow norms), and pooling risks one class mechanically dominating "high $\lambda$" rather than the split reflecting real cross-sectional dispersion within each class.

     than trusting `cmcRank`; drop rows with null/≤0 market cap.
     **Rationale:** matches the spec wording exactly and is robust to any stored-rank quirks.
     **Downstream impact:** ranks are internally consistent with the market-cap values used
     for entry decisions.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-23T21:19:50.269Z

Universe size first, since that's the most direct answer: **1,939 in-universe assets** — 633 coins, 448 governance tokens, 858 "other" (memes/utility tokens excluded from the hypothesis tests by construction). That's unchanged from Phase 0B; Phase 1 builds on top of it rather than altering it.

How the λ build went:

Mid-session you redirected the sourcing strategy — instead of pulling λ inputs from DeFiLlama (an aggregator), you asked for canonical on-chain sources directly ("etherscan or other chain main data source... to ensure we are getting information from the real source"). That became the defining constraint: DeFiLlama got demoted to a metadata registry (asset → contract/Snapshot-space lookup only), and every actual λ number now comes from raw Etherscan event logs or Snapshot's own API.

Source reality check: Snapshot's GraphQL API and CMC historical data worked free with no key. Etherscan V2 needed a key (you supplied one, stored gitignored). beaconcha.in, Boardroom, and Tally — all previously usable — are now paywalled (401s). More importantly, **no free RPC serves archived historical state**, so every Channel-1 number had to be reconstructed from immutable event logs rather than balance lookups at a past block.

Channel-by-channel results:
- **Staking/locking**: ETH's beacon-deposit-contract method is validated (matches public figures: 2.17M ETH staked Dec 2020, 5.2M May 2021) but the full series is only partially run (18 of the needed months so far — it's a long, resumable job). Six vote-escrow tokens (CRV, CVX, FXS, AAVE, SUSHI, YFI) are fully built and validated to within <3% of live on-chain balances. Everything else — the 600+ non-EVM coins (Solana, Cosmos, Cardano, etc.) — has zero staking coverage; an Etherscan key can't reach them.
- **Holding duration**: not built at all. Flagged explicitly as a gap rather than faked with a weak proxy — this is the channel that would have given early-sample (pre-2020) coins any λ at all.
- **Voting engagement**: the strongest channel — 55 DAOs mapped, 51 with valid token-weighted turnout, 1,178 asset-months from mid-2020 to mid-2026.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-23T21:30:55.464Z

No, you don't need to pay anything — the free Etherscan API key you already provided ("AFA Paper") covers everything that was actually built. The confusion is worth untangling though, because two different things got conflated in the report's source table:

**What's free and what was used**: Etherscan's free tier gives unlimited access to event logs (the `DepositEvent` logs for ETH staking, `Transfer` logs for the 6 vote-escrow tokens). That's exactly the method used — reconstructing locked/staked amounts by replaying logs rather than querying a balance directly. Free, no paywall.

**What's NOT free anywhere — not just Etherscan**: querying a contract's *historical state* at a past block (e.g., "what was this balance on 2021-05-01?") needs an archive node, and no free provider serves that — not Etherscan, not Cloudflare/Ankr/PublicNode/1rpc either. Etherscan's free `eth_call` doesn't even error on this — it silently just returns *today's* value, which is worse than a paywall because it looks like it worked. That's why the team avoided state reads entirely and rebuilt everything from logs instead. So this isn't "pay Etherscan and the problem goes away" — it's a fundamentally different (harder) method that the free tier just doesn't offer, period.

**On DeFiLlama**: it wasn't dropped because it's unreliable for missing data generally — it's still in the source table, just for a narrower job: mapping each asset's `cmc_id` to its contract address or Snapshot space (a lookup table, not a data feed). The actual staking/locking *numbers* in `lambda_panel.csv` all come from Etherscan logs per your direction. DeFiLlama isn't supplying any λ values.

One real limitation to flag: Etherscan only covers EVM chains. The 600+ non-EVM coins (Solana, Cosmos, Cardano, etc.) can't be reached with this key at all — not a cost issue, a coverage issue. Closing that gap means per-chain explorers (Solscan, Mintscan, etc.), not a paid Etherscan tier.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-24T15:36:05.466Z

Worth grounding this in the project's own history first: the 2026-06-10 theory session (`session_002_2026-06-10_theory.md`) already touched this exact question and landed somewhere specific — it's not that your TVL instinct is new or mistaken, it's that the project's thinking on this has moved since then.

That session's "TVL Disambiguation" note drew a sharp line: TVL-as-λ (staked coins, a supply/conviction measure) for coins, versus **TVL-as-PQ ("nominal GDP analog") for tokens**. So at the theory stage, TVL-for-tokens was explicitly endorsed, not just your instinct — it was the team's own framing. `DATA_SPECIFICATION.md` (written twelve days later, June 22) is where that loosened: it asks for "DEX volume, total fees, or active-user counts" for tokens and doesn't mention TVL at all. That's a real, undocumented drift between two of the project's own source documents, and the Phase 2 memo is essentially surfacing it without realizing there's a paper trail behind it.

Here's why I think the June 22 spec's version is the more defensible one, and it comes straight from the paper's own framework rather than from "the spec said so": this is a *Quantity Theory of Money* paper. M·V = P·Q is the identity in the name. P·Q, by construction, is a nominal flow — that's not a modeling choice, it's accounting. TVL is a stock (M, the capital sitting in the system), not P·Q. Using TVL as PQ is implicitly assuming a constant, unmodeled velocity (PQ = TVL × 1), which collapses a variable the framework treats as economically meaningful into a fixed parameter. The June 10 framing called TVL "GDP-like" as a rough proxy when nothing better was on the table; the June 22 spec, written once the team was thinking about actual construction, correctly tightened that to genuine flows. So I'd treat this less as "overriding your instinct" and more as "the spec already caught and fixed the looseness in the original theory note — worth saying so explicitly in the decisions log so it doesn't look like an accident later." That lines up with the memo's Decision 1 recommendation (A): fees/DEX-volume as PQ, TVL kept as a side column for an MC/TVL robustness cut, not as NVT_GL itself.

On Decision 2 (coin PQ), I'd add one wrinkle the memo doesn't quite name: even setting the archive-access wall aside, raw "transaction value summed from the chain" isn't as clean as it sounds for an account-based chain like ETH. A simple value transfer uses the tx's `value` field, but most of ETH's actual economic activity today is smart-contract calls (swaps, transfers, mints) where `value` is often 0 and the real value movement happens inside the contract logic — so even with full archive access, summing `value` would understate true throughput. Gas fees side-step that (you pay gas regardless of whether value moved via `value` or internal contract state), which is part of why I think (A) chain fees holds up as a genuine "revealed throughput" proxy, not just a fallback — though it's worth being explicit in the writeup that fees are a small, congestion-dependent slice of value moved, not volume itself; a chain can have high genuine usage and low fees (efficient L2s) or the reverse.

One concrete addition to option (C): for BTC specifically — a pure UTXO chain, so this problem doesn't apply — blockchain.com's free public charts API has a daily "estimated transaction volume (USD)" series back to ~2010. That's a free, already-aggregated, genuinely scalable cross-check for the flagship coin, better than what the memo found for coin-age. Worth having the next session check that before settling for fees-only on BTC.

Where do you want to land — are you persuaded on (A) for both, or is there a reason you want TVL to stay in the token side (e.g., if you think capital-at-risk is the conviction signal you actually care about, in which case that might belong on the λ side instead, not PQ)?

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-24T15:46:35.198Z

The research lines up cleanly, and it's worth quoting because it's about as direct an answer as you'll get: DeFiLlama — the platform you'd actually be pulling from — defines its `fees` metric explicitly as "the total amount paid by users for using the service... the top-line number that shows how much the protocol is facilitating in economic activity." Not TVL. Fees is their own operational definition of "economic activity."

That's not an isolated choice. Token Terminal (the platform that popularized P/S ratios for crypto — literally MC/Sales, the closest existing analog to MC/PQ) defines Fees as "how much economic activity the protocol is capturing," with Revenue as the narrower subset the protocol actually retains. Their published P/S ratio uses revenue or fees in the denominator — never TVL. Artemis frames it the same way: fees = "total value paid by users to use a platform or service," and their Terminal product lists Revenue, Fees, and TVL as three separate, parallel metrics — never one standing in for another. And reaching outside crypto entirely, GMV (the e-commerce/marketplace equivalent — Uber, Etsy, etc.) is defined as "total value of transactions processed... over a specific period" — again a flow, again never a stock of capital sitting in the system.

So across every aggregator that does this for a living, "economic activity" is consistently a flow term (fees, revenue, or GMV/volume), and TVL is consistently tracked as a separate, complementary number — useful, reported, but never substituted in as the activity measure. That's a strong piece of external validation for Decision 1: it's not just the spec's preference, it's the field's convention.

On "average daily TVL per month as the flow" — I want to flag a technical issue with that specific move, because the intuition behind it is actually right even though the mechanics don't quite get there. Time-averaging a stock still gives you a stock (same units — dollars sitting in the pool — just smoothed against end-of-month noise). It doesn't acquire flow units just by being averaged. What *does* convert a stock into a flow, and what your underlying intuition is actually reaching for, is exactly the M·V = P·Q identity this paper is named after: PQ = TVL × velocity, where velocity is how many times that locked capital turns over per period. And — this is the practical catch — velocity is computed as Volume/TVL or Fees/TVL. So unwinding that gives you the volume or fees figure back directly; you can't get PQ from TVL alone without already having the flow number as an input. TVL isn't the wrong intuition, it's the wrong half of the identity — it's the "M," not the "PQ."

That said, I'd keep that capital-turnover idea rather than discard it: Volume/TVL (or Fees/TVL) is a real, separately meaningful diagnostic — sometimes called "capital efficiency" in DeFi analytics — and it's a genuinely interesting auxiliary variable (low turnover = capital parked but not very active, which might say something adjacent to conviction). Worth keeping as a reported side metric alongside MC/TVL, distinct from PQ itself.

One more data-quality point in TVL's favor of staying out of the core PQ measure: a BIS working paper specifically flags that TVL methodology is inconsistent and largely self-reported across aggregators, with no standardization — a real verifiability problem if it were load-bearing in the paper's main result, separate from the stock-vs-flow issue.

Net: I'd finalize Decision 1 as fees (DeFiLlama's `fees`, matching their own "economic activity" framing — not `revenue`, since revenue is the protocol's discretionary take-rate cut and can jump around for governance reasons unrelated to actual usage), with TVL and a Volume/TVL turnover ratio both kept as side columns for robustness and as a citable bridge back to your original instinct. Does that resolve it for you, or do you want to push further on revenue vs. fees specifically?

Sources:
- [DeFiLlama — Data Definitions & Metrics Glossary](https://defillama.com/data-definitions)
- [Token Terminal — Fees](https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/metrics/fees)
- [Token Terminal — The price to sales ratio (P/S)](https://tokenterminal.com/resources/articles/the-price-to-sales-ratio-p-s)
- [Artemis — Crypto Revenue: a standard and consistent definition for value accrual to token holders](https://research.artemisanalytics.com/p/crypto-revenue-a-standard-and-consistent)
- [Artemis Terminal — Compare Crypto Protocol Revenue, Fees, TVL, and On-Chain Metrics](https://about.artemis.ai/products/terminal)
- [BIS — Towards verifiability of total value locked (TVL) in decentralized finance](https://www.bis.org/publ/work1268.htm)
- [Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) Explained](https://startupik.com/gross-merchandise-value-gmv-explained-the-marketplace-growth-metric/)
