**Bottom line: TEA itself won't proxy your 96 tokens — but the catalog behind it has real, per-protocol candidates worth checking before you pay anything.**

**1. TEA is chain-level, not app-level.** It's computed per blockchain (Ethereum, Solana, Avalanche, etc.) as Chain Fees+MEV + Settlement Volume + App Fees. Since almost all of your 96 are application/protocol tokens, not chains, subscribing "to get TEA for token X" doesn't work — there's no per-app TEA number to pull.

**2. Documentation is public — no subscription needed to check fit.** Artemis's Asset Metrics Catalog (`artemis.ai/docs/data-reference/asset-metrics-catalog`) lists every metric field tracked per asset, and I read it directly without logging in. The real question isn't "does Artemis have TEA for token X," it's "does the catalog list a flow/volume field for token X" — and that varies protocol by protocol, same discipline Phase 2c already used for DeFiLlama.

**3. What I found cross-checking it against your gap list** (catalog read alphabetically Aave→Magic Eden — roughly two-thirds of the full list; Chrome wasn't connected to pull the rest live):

- **Real hit: Avantis (AVNT)** — rejected in Phase 2c as `turnover_undefensible` because DeFiLlama's derivatives vertical is paywalled. Artemis catalogs it directly with `PERP_VOLUME`, `PERP_DAU`, `DEX_VOLUMES`, `FEES`, `REVENUE`, `TVL` — a genuine transacted-value field, not a workaround.
- **Pattern, not yet confirmed by name:** every derivatives/perps app in the catalog (GMX, Hyperliquid, Jupiter, dYdX, Drift, Bluefin, ApeX, Aevo) carries `PERP_VOLUME`/`PERP_FEES`, and every bridge app (Across, deBridge, Axelar, LayerZero) carries `BRIDGE_VOLUME`/`BRIDGE_FEES`/`BRIDGE_TXNS`. If your remaining bridge tokens (Wormhole, Synapse, Celer, Biconomy, pNetwork, Ren) and derivatives tokens (DDX, MIR, MYX...) follow the same pattern, several "bridge_vol_paywalled" / "turnover_undefensible" rejections could flip — but I couldn't confirm by name; those fall in the back half of the alphabet I couldn't retrieve (page truncates at ~487 lines on every fetch attempt, and Chrome's not connected right now to load the full live page).
- **Confirmed absent — no help regardless of tier:** Hakka Finance, HXRO, Keep3r (KP3R), Linear Finance (LINA), Keep Network, DerivaDEX (DDX). Not in Artemis's catalog at all.
- **No new lever:** Convex Finance (CVX) only has `FEES`/`REVENUE`/`TVL`/`NET_DEPOSITS` — same TVL×APY situation Phase 2c already found, Artemis doesn't add a settlement-volume field here.
- AAVE, LDO, GNS (already viable via Dune) have full Artemis coverage too — useful as a cross-check source, not a new gap-filler.

**4. Pricing.** Lite = free forever (3 charts, 3 CSV downloads/month). Pro = $300/mo or $3,000/yr. Enterprise = custom. A discounted **student subscription** exists — email `team@artemis.xyz` with an academic address, directly relevant given UTSA. **ASSISTANT** 2026-06-25T22:51:39.032Z

Good news: this is already a solved question in the repo, from the Etherscan pilot back in session 012 (`03_data/PHASE2_PQ_PILOT_REPORT.md`). Two distinct problems were found, and they need different fixes — paying for speed only fixes one of them.

**Misprints** — literal corrupted data points. The pilot pulled every AAVE transfer for May 2026 and got a raw sum of $8.2×10¹⁹, which is physically impossible (AAVE's whole supply is 15.4M tokens). Cause: 6 of 116,910 transfers carried sentinel garbage values, one exactly 10¹⁸ tokens — 65 billion times the entire supply. These are trivial to throw out: drop anything above some sane ceiling (e.g., larger than circulating supply). Doing that took AAVE from $8.2×10¹⁹ down to a clean $2.75B. This part of your plan — "collect data and throw out the misprints" — already works and is proven.

**Intra-account/wash-trading overestimation** — a different, harder problem. Even after removing the misprints, raw transfer volume still counts wallet-to-wallet shuffling that isn't a genuine economic exchange between two distinct parties: an exchange moving tokens between its own hot wallets, a protocol rebalancing its own treasury across contracts, a user moving tokens between two wallets they control. None of that is a misprint — it's real, valid data — but it inflates the implied "P×Q" relative to actual transacted value. This is the classic critique of raw on-chain volume as an NVT proxy, and it's flagged in your own `DATA_SPECIFICATION.md` §6 as a known landmine.

Here's the part that didn't fully come through before: **for most of your 96 tokens, neither problem is actually the binding one.** UNI's transfer log had *zero* misprints and presumably minimal wash noise — it was clean. But it was still **46.6× smaller** than Uniswap's real DEX swap volume ($0.79B vs. $36.75B) and only **0.30 correlated** with it day-to-day. The reason: a swap moves the *traded pair* through *pool* contracts — it doesn't move the UNI token at all. Same logic hits AAVE: even the clean $2.75B is governance-token movement, unconnected to Aave's actual lending throughput, which is denominated in USDC/ETH, not AAVE. This is a structural object-mismatch, not noise — no amount of misprint-scrubbing or wash-filtering turns a governance token's transfer log into the protocol's real throughput.

That distinction matters directly for your "pay for speed" idea. Current Etherscan API tiers (checked live):

| Tier | Price/mo | Rate limit | Daily cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 3 calls/s | 100K |
| Lite | $49 | 5 calls/s | 100K |
| Standard | $199 | 10 calls/s | 200K |
| Advanced | $299 | 20 calls/s | 500K |
| Professional | $399 | 30 calls/s | 1M |
| Pro Plus | $899 | 30 calls/s | 1.5M + address-metadata endpoint |

The pilot's extrapolation: full-history pull across the ~127 DeFi-slug token panel needs ~1.75M `getLogs` calls — about 17.5 days at the free tier's 100K/day cap, shrinking to roughly 9/3.5/2 days on Standard/Advanced/Professional. So paying for speed genuinely does compress the *cost* axis. It does nothing for the *validity* axis — you'd just pull the same wrong object faster.

So paying only pays off for tokens where the protocol's own token transfers really are the transacted-value object — not governance/pool tokens of AMMs, lending markets, perps, or bridges (which is most of the 96). It could be worth it for a token whose entire model is direct peer-to-peer settlement in the token itself (Zeebu/ZBU is the one candidate worth checking on this basis — it's a B2B payments-settlement token, not a pool governance token). Before spending anything, I'd run a quick per-token pass on the 96 — same discipline Phase 2c used — asking specifically "is this token literally the unit of value being exchanged, or is it a governance/LP token sitting on top of pools denominated in other assets?" Only the first group benefits from Etherscan at any tier. I haven't done that categorization yet — want me to run it before you commit anything?

For the wash-trading piece specifically, the realistic free options are: drop self-transfers (from==to), cap by percentile/supply-ceiling (proven, as above), and cross-check totals against DeFiLlama as a sanity ceiling. Actually identifying same-entity wallet clusters (exchange hot-wallet labels) requires Etherscan's Address Metadata endpoint, which only ships on the $899/mo Pro Plus tier — and even that just gives you labels, not a wash-trading filter; you'd still be building the exclusion logic yourself.

You're half right, and the half that's off is the important half — let me separate it cleanly using the AAVE/UNI numbers we already have.

**The coin point is correct.** For BTC/ETH wallet-to-wallet transfers, a genuine transfer between two different people *is* real economic activity — that's the standard coin-side PQ logic, and it's consistent with the project's own spec. The actual obstacle there isn't conceptual, it's technical: native ETH/BTC transfers aren't `Transfer` events you can pull from logs — you need archive-node tracing, which is a separate, harder wall the pilot already flagged. Wash trading at the coin level is really about *same-entity* hops (an exchange moving between its own wallets), which is a labeling problem, not a contract-vs-wallet problem.

**The token point needs one correction: it's not "the token to/from the contract" — it's "the right asset to/from the contract."** Here's the AAVE/UNI case again, but framed your way:

If you restrict to AAVE token transfers in/out of Aave's own contracts, you'd mostly capture people staking AAVE into the Safety Module. That's a real number — but it measures *governance-token staking*, not lending throughput. Aave's actual economic activity (loans, deposits, borrows) is denominated in USDC, WETH, DAI — assets that move through Aave's *Lending Pool* contracts, never touching the AAVE token at all. So "contract in/out" is the right *technique*, but you have to apply it to the assets actually flowing through the protocol, not to the protocol's own governance token.

Same story for Uniswap: a swap moves the two *paired* assets (say USDC and WETH) into and out of a *pool* contract — UNI itself never moves. Tracking "UNI transfers to/from Uniswap's contracts" would again just catch UNI staking/locking, missing the $36.75B of real swap volume entirely.

So your instinct — anchor PQ to contract-level flows — is exactly right, but executing it for real means: (1) enumerate every contract address that constitutes the protocol (one lending pool is easy; a DEX with one pool per trading pair can mean thousands, often spun up dynamically by a factory contract), (2) for each contract, identify which asset(s) passing through it represent real economic value (almost never the protocol's own governance token), (3) pull `Transfer` events of *those* assets in/out of *those* addresses, not the governance token's log.

That's not a small filter on top of what we already pulled — it's a different, larger build, protocol by protocol. And it's exactly what Dune's pre-decoded event tables and DeFiLlama's adapters already do under the hood, which is why Phase 2c's 5 viable tokens (AAVE, STRK, LDO, GNS, SUN) came from Dune spells rather than raw Etherscan — those spells already encode "here's the right contract, here's the right asset" per protocol.

Where doing this yourself from raw Etherscan would actually be worth it: protocols with a small, fixed number of contracts and an obvious single settlement asset — a single-vault yield farm, or a bridge's lock/mint escrow contract (bridge volume is literally "asset in/out of the escrow," which maps onto your idea almost exactly). Where it's not worth it: multi-pool AMMs, multi-market lending, leveraged perps (collateral-in ≠ notional traded) — there you'd be rebuilding a DeFiLlama adapter from scratch for one token.

Want me to scope which of the remaining tokens have the "few contracts, one obvious asset" shape (so a from-scratch build is actually tractable) versus the "many pools/markets" shape (where it's not worth redoing)?

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-25T23:01:15.197Z

Right — that's the correct version, and it lines up with how the paper already separates λ (governance/engagement, from UNI) from PQ (transacted value, from the pool's actual flows). Two real snags before this becomes a build, both visible in your own ETH/USDT example:

**1. Raw Transfer-log summing can't tell a swap from a liquidity add/remove.** Both move ETH and USDT in or out of the same pool contract address. If someone adds liquidity (deposits ETH+USDT to mint LP tokens) or removes it, that's a capital-stock movement, not transacted value — but a generic `Transfer` pull on the contract address sees both as identical "money moved to/from this address" events. To isolate genuine trade flow you need to decode the pool's specific `Swap` event (which is tagged separately from `Mint`/`Burn`), not just sum ERC-20 Transfers. That's exactly the layer Dune/DeFiLlama already built — it's why their numbers are clean and a raw-log sum wouldn't be.

**2. One pair, many contracts.** "The ETH/USDT pool" isn't one address — Uniswap V3 alone has a separate contract per fee tier (0.01%/0.05%/0.3%/1%) for that pair, plus V2, plus every other DEX that lists ETH/USDT. To get a protocol's total volume (what actually feeds PQ) you'd need to enumerate every pool contract it has ever deployed via the factory's `PoolCreated` events, then decode each one. Native ETH also doesn't emit `Transfer` events at all — most pools hold WETH instead, but if a pool genuinely handles native ETH you hit the same archive-trace wall as coin-side PQ.

None of this is a paid-tier problem — it's a decoding-logic problem, so faster Etherscan calls don't shrink it. Where this actually pays off depends on protocol type, applied to your remaining gap categories:

- **Bridges** — best fit. Bridge volume is often literally defined as asset-in/asset-out of an escrow contract, with no liquidity-add conflation (unless it's a liquidity-pool-style bridge like Across, which has the exact same LP-vs-trade ambiguity as an AMM).
- **Derivatives** — poor fit. Collateral moving into a margin/vault contract isn't the leveraged notional traded; this would systematically undercount perps volume by the leverage factor. You'd need the protocol's own `Trade`/position-event log, not transfer sums.
- **Lending** — this is already solved the right way: Dune's `Pool_evt_Supply/Borrow/Repay` tables for AAVE etc. already do exactly this contract-flow decoding for free. Any further lending gaps need the same kind of decoded-event table, not raw Etherscan.
- **Farm/Yield** — doesn't really apply; most of those 28 are dead contracts with nothing to pull regardless of method.

So the bridge tokens are the one category where building this from scratch on raw Etherscan looks genuinely worth scoping. Want me to check which of the bridge tokens have a small, fixed escrow-contract structure (vs. an LP-pool structure) before you spend anything on a paid tier?

2. Key Technical Concepts:

   - **PQ (transacted value) proxy methodology** — the paper's core empirical task: finding a defensible transacted-value series for each of 127 tokens/coins. Established waterfall (DATA_DECISIONS_LOG.md Entry 32, referenced not re-read this window): DeFiLlama sector-appropriate reported volume (DEX/swap, perps notional, borrow/origination) as primary source; TVL and fees as side diagnostics; Dune spells as secondary source (used for AAVE/STRK/LDO/GNS/SUN in Phase 2c); raw Etherscan Transfer logs only as an occasional spot-check, never primary.
   - **Governance-token-transfer ≠ protocol-throughput mismatch** — the central finding of `PHASE2_PQ_PILOT_REPORT.md`: a protocol's own governance/utility token (UNI, AAVE) is structurally the wrong object to sum for PQ, because the protocol's real economic activity (swaps, loans) moves *other* assets (the traded pair, the borrowed stablecoin) through *pool/vault* contracts — the governance token itself rarely moves during that activity. Concretely: UNI transfer volume ($0.79B, May 2026) was 46.6× smaller than Uniswap's real DEX swap volume ($36.75B, DeFiLlama), with only 0.30 daily correlation, despite UNI's transfer data being completely clean (zero misprints). AAVE's raw transfer sum was corrupted by 6 sentinel-value outliers (one of exactly 10¹⁸ tokens, 65 billion× the actual circulating supply) inflating it to a physically-impossible $8.2×10¹⁹; after removing those 6, "clean" volume = $2.75B — but even this clean number is still governance-token movement, unconnected to Aave's lending throughput (denominated in USDC/ETH, not AAVE).
   - **Misprints vs. wash-trading/intra-account overestimation — two distinct, differently-solvable problems:**
     - *Misprints*: literal corrupted/sentinel data points (non-economic placeholder values). Trivially filterable via a sanity ceiling (e.g., drop any transfer exceeding circulating supply) — already proven on AAVE.
     - *Wash-trading / intra-account movement* (per `DATA_SPECIFICATION.md` §6, line 314: "Wash trading / exchange-internal transfers inflating raw on-chain transaction volume (PQ for coins) — a known critique of traditional NVT"): real, valid transfers that don't represent genuine economic exchange between distinct counterparties (e.g., an exchange shuffling between its own hot wallets, a user moving between their own wallets). Harder to clean — free options are self-transfer exclusion (from==to) and percentile/supply-ceiling capping; identifying same-entity address clusters requires labeled data, which on Etherscan only ships via the $899/mo Pro Plus tier's Address Metadata endpoint (and even that only gives labels, not a ready-made wash-trading filter).
   - **Contract-address-flow methodology (user's proposed refinement, now clarified)** — track Transfer events of the *relevant paired/settlement asset(s)* (not the protocol's own governance token) moving in/out of the protocol's own contract address(es) as the genuine PQ measure. User's clarifying example: for a Uniswap ETH/USDT pool, the PQ is ETH and USDT flows in/out of that pool contract — not UNI movement. This is conceptually correct and exactly what Dune's decoded event tables / DeFiLlama's per-protocol adapters already compute under the hood (which is why Phase 2c's 5 viable tokens came from Dune spells rather than raw Etherscan). Executing this from scratch via raw Etherscan (for protocols with no Dune/DeFiLlama coverage) requires, per protocol: (1) enumerating every relevant contract address (trivial for a single lending pool; potentially thousands for a multi-pair AMM, often requiring factory-contract `PoolCreated`-style event discovery), (2) identifying which 1-2 assets are the actual settlement/paired assets for each contract, (3) pulling Transfer events of *those* assets to/from *those* addresses. This is a materially larger build than filtering one token's own Transfer log, and is effectively re-deriving a DeFiLlama/Dune adapter from scratch.
   - **λ (lambda)** — a separate variable in the paper's theoretical framework (referenced in completed Task #7, "λ-as-index note," and Task #8, replacing an "F() hand-wave with rigorous continuum-of-agents derivation"). User's most recent message establishes that governance tokens like UNI feed into λ calculations, not into PQ — i.e., PQ and λ draw on different on-chain objects for the same protocol.
   - **Etherscan API current pricing/rate limits** (fetched live this window from `etherscan.io/apis` and `docs.etherscan.io/resources/rate-limits`, June 2026):
     | Tier | Price/mo | Rate limit | Daily cap | API Pro endpoints |
     |---|---|---|---|---|
     | Free | $0 | 3 calls/s | 100,000 | Not available |
     | Lite | $49 | 5 calls/s | 100,000 | Not available |
     | Standard | $199 | 10 calls/s | 200,000 | Available |
     | Advanced | $299 | 20 calls/s | 500,000 | Available |

     | Pro Plus | $899 | 30 calls/s | 1,500,000 | Available + Address Metadata endpoint (1 app license only) |
     | Enterprise | custom | unmetered | unmetered | Available, SLA-backed |
     Quarterly billing = 10% off, annual = 15% off (rates shown above are monthly list price). **Key conclusion drawn: paying for a higher tier compresses the *cost/throughput* axis (full-panel multi-year history: ~17.5 days at free-tier 100K/day cap → ~9/3.5/2 days at Standard/Advanced/Professional) but does nothing for the *validity* axis** — it only lets you pull the same (potentially wrong) object faster.
   - **Artemis Analytics findings** (carried forward, now resolved/closed per Task #64): TEA is chain-level (`Chain Fees & MEV + Settlement Volume + Application Fees`), not per-app; the public Asset Metrics Catalog (`artemis.ai/docs/data-reference/asset-metrics-catalog`) lists per-asset metric fields without requiring a subscription; confirmed hit on Avantis (AVNT: `PERP_VOLUME`, `PERP_DAU`, `DEX_VOLUMES`, `FEES`, `REVENUE`, `TVL`); confirmed absences (Hakka Finance, HXRO, Keep3r/KP3R, Linear Finance/LINA, Keep Network, DerivaDEX/DDX); no new lever for Convex Finance (CVX); pricing tiers (Lite free, Pro $300/mo or $3,000/yr, Enterprise custom, student discount via team@artemis.xyz); caveat that "Protocol and Stablecoin Analytics" requires contacting Artemis sales rather than self-serve Pro signup. Catalog fetch was persistently truncated at 487 lines/~71,200 characters on every attempt (web_fetch twice, Chrome MCP unavailable, Nimble CLI/MCP unavailable) — coverage confirmed only through "Magic Eden" alphabetically (roughly two-thirds of the full catalog); tokens N-Z (Wormhole/W, Synapse/SYN, Zeebu/ZBU, Velodrome/VELO, Mirror/MIR, MYX, Numeraire/NMR, Harvest Finance/FARM, Starknet/STRK, SUN, bridge tokens BICO/CELR/MERL/PNT/REN, Stake DAO/STAKE) remain unconfirmed in the catalog.
   - **Coin-side wash-trading distinction** — user correctly noted that for coins (BTC/ETH), a genuine wallet-to-wallet transfer between two distinct economic agents *is* real activity (consistent with the project's own spec) — the actual obstacle for coin-side PQ isn't conceptual, it's technical: native ETH/BTC transfers require archive-node tracing rather than `Transfer` event logs (a separate, harder wall already noted in the pilot's closing section, distinct from any wash-trading question).

Confirmed: your refined framing is exactly right, and matches what DeFiLlama/Dune already compute under the hood. The research is saved as `03_data/CONTRACT_EVENT_TAXONOMY_RESEARCH.md` and logged in `time_log.md`.

Key findings:

- It really does collapse to ~6-7 recognizable patterns, not 96 bespoke investigations — DEX/AMM (`Swap` event, excluding `Mint`/`Burn` liquidity events), Lending (`Supply`/`Borrow`/`Repay`/`Withdraw`), Derivatives (notional field inside the position event, not raw collateral), Bridges (lock-and-mint vs. liquidity-pool style — different fit), Liquid Staking, and Yield Vaults (increasingly standardized via ERC-4626).
- Contract enumeration ("all addresses running this code") is a solved problem for almost every category: a Factory contract's creation-event log (e.g. Uniswap's `PairCreated`) lists every instance — no bytecode archaeology needed. EIP-1167 clone detection and Etherscan's Similar Contract Search cover the rest.
- The biggest practical shortcut: Dune auto-decodes any source-verified contract's events into raw tables the moment it's indexed — no hand-built "spell" required. That turns this from "write an Etherscan ABI decoder" into "find the verified address, write one Dune SQL query," much closer to the AAVE/LDO/GNS work already done than a from-scratch build.
- Applied to your remaining gap categories: Bridges and DEX/AMM gaps are the best fit; Derivatives is workable but bespoke per protocol; Farm/Yield mostly doesn't apply (dead contracts).

The doc ends with a 4-step scoping process (re-tag the 96 by category → quick Etherscan verified/Factory check → check Dune for an existing decoded table → only then write bespoke queries) — all runs on tools you already have free access to.

Sources: [Uniswap V2/V3 docs](https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v2/reference/smart-contracts/factory), [Aave V3 Pool docs](https://aave.com/docs/aave-v3/smart-contracts/pool), [Compound V2 docs](https://docs.compound.finance/v2/ctokens/), [ERC-4626 spec](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626), [Wormhole Token Bridge docs](https://wormhole.com/docs/products/token-bridge/guides/token-bridge-contracts/), [Across docs](https://docs.across.to/reference/tracking-events), [GMX V2 docs](https://docs.gmx.io/docs/api/contracts-v2/), [Lido docs](https://docs.lido.fi/contracts/lido/), [EIP-1167 spec](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1167), [Etherscan Similar Contract Search](https://etherscan.io/find-similar-contracts), [Dune Spellbook](https://github.com/duneanalytics/spellbook).

2. Key Technical Concepts:

   - **SoV/MoE decomposition (paper's existing core framework, per `05_paper/main.tex`):** Market cap MC decomposes into a Medium-of-Exchange component MC_MoE = M(1-λ) and a Store-of-Value residual MC_SoV = Mλ, where λ = M_locked/M (fraction of supply locked/staked). The SoV/MoE ratio simplifies mechanically to λ/(1-λ), directly observable without velocity estimation. This decomposition is currently presented in the paper as a single unified accounting identity applied across "the economy" (Section 1, lines 33-46; formal derivation Appendix lines 459-491) — i.e., not yet explicitly bifurcated into a coin-specific vs. token-specific version of the *decomposition itself*, even though the *mechanism/interpretation* of λ already is bifurcated (see next point). This is the precise locus of the user's critique.
   - **λ's dual theoretical grounding (already asymmetric in the paper's existing text, lines 108-150):** For native coins (ETH, SOL, etc.), high λ is grounded in three complementary traditions: (1) monetary search theory (Kiyotaki & Wright 1993; Lagos & Wright 2005) — money emerges as a coordination equilibrium, high λ is the on-chain-observable signal of coordination commitment; (2) convenience yield (Sockin 2020; Krishnamurthy & Vissing-Jorgensen 2012) — non-pecuniary benefit of holding; (3) seigniorage (Cong 2024 staking) — staking decision reveals belief that staking income plus price appreciation exceeds the opportunity cost of locking. For governance/utility tokens, λ carries a *different* signal — explicitly NOT grounded in monetary theory: "Staking a governance token into a DAO contract renders it illiquid... An agent who voluntarily incurs this illiquidity cost reveals a preference for future [platform value]" — this is costly-signaling logic per Spence (1973), confirmed again at lines 277-280 ("the monetary search-theoretic view of λ as a coordination signal... for coins, and with the costly-signaling logic of Spence (1973) for governance tokens"). The threshold-crossing formula for λ_t = H(b_t + θ_{t+1}) is identical in form across both asset types (lines 269-284); only the composition of b_t (seigniorage vs. fee-share-or-zero) and φ_i (pure liquidity cost vs. lock cost plus engagement cost) differs by asset class.
   - **Growth-Levelized NVT ratio (paper's existing Y-axis measure, currently used for BOTH coins and tokens):** NVT_GL,t = MC_t / PQ_t* (market cap over a PMT-discounted-cash-flow-style present value of expected transaction stream). Per the paper's own explicit framing (lines 154-167, 356-394), NVT_GL carries **no independent theoretical prediction for returns** — its sole role is as a *conditioning variable* indicating how much of λ's conviction signal (δ_t, the "absorbed fraction") the market has already priced in. Formally: p_t = p_t^fund(1+δ_t); higher current price relative to fundamental transaction-based value ⇒ higher δ_t ⇒ higher NVT_GL,t. Expected return from t to t+1 is proportional to the *unabsorbed* signal λ_t(1-δ_t), so predictive power of λ_t is decreasing in NVT_GL,t (Proposition 2, lines 375-377; Hypothesis 2, lines 379-383).
   - **Quadrant Portfolio (paper's existing 2x2 framework, lines 396-411):** Star = high λ/(1-λ) AND low NVT_GL (best expected returns); Avoid = low λ/(1-λ) AND high NVT_GL (worst expected returns). Hypothesis 3: long Star / short Avoid portfolio, rebalanced monthly, generates positive alpha after controlling for market, size, momentum.

User's caveat on NV/TVL: "The only issue becomes that TVL to revenue channel is different for different tokens. ## Evaluation of your coin/token critique

You're right, and the paper's own appendix proves it more cleanly than I expected. Look at the derivation: `MC_SoV/MC_MoE = λ/(1-λ)` — `PQ` cancels out completely. The SoV/MoE ratio is a pure supply-side identity (locked share over free share); it doesn't actually depend on whether the free-circulating supply functions as a medium of exchange at all. So your instinct to keep λ/(1-λ) for tokens is correct on the strongest possible grounds: the math never needed the MoE story to begin with. Nothing about the *methodology* has to change.

What does need fixing is the *narrative* wrapped around it. Lines 130-137 of `main.tex` currently argue UNI "is the monetary instrument of the Uniswap protocol economy," analogous to the dollar and U.S. GDP — and cites Cong-Li-Wang (2021) and Schilling-Uhlig (2019) to support that. But Cong-Li-Wang's actual mechanism is about tokens *required* to transact on a platform (gas tokens, pay-per-use tokens); Schilling-Uhlig models a coin competing as currency. Neither describes UNI, where you don't need to hold or spend UNI to swap on Uniswap. And your own project already has the empirical knife for this: the Phase 2 PQ pilot found UNI transfer volume runs at about 1/46.6th of real Uniswap swap volume, weakly correlated — direct evidence the governance token isn't carrying the protocol's transactional flow at all. So the fix is narrow: relabel λ/(1-λ) as a conviction ratio (SoV/MoE retained only for coins, where the monetary-theory grounding is real), and drop or scope that specific protocol-currency analogy to genuine utility/payment tokens rather than governance-only ones. Nothing else in the paper moves.

## Multiples research

Saved as `01_literature/VALUATION_MULTIPLES_LITERATURE_REVIEW.md`. Highlights:

Damodaran has an existing four-bucket framework (assets/commodities/currencies/collectibles) that independently validates your split: only cash-flow-generating "assets" can be *valued*; currencies (he puts Bitcoin here) can only be *priced*. A token with real or plausible fee-accrual rights sits closer to his "asset" bucket — which is exactly why NV/TVL, NV/Revenue, NV/Fee make more sense for tokens than the currency-style NVT_GL does.

His P/B work gives a precise analogue for NV/TVL: bank P/B is driven by ROE relative to cost of equity, and comparing P/B across banks without controlling for ROE is the classic mistake. TVL is your "book value"; the missing control is Fees/TVL or Revenue/TVL — your project's own Phase 2c diagnostic already measured ~1,455× dispersion in that ratio across the lending cohort, which is empirical proof your "different universe" caveat is real, not hypothetical.

On the crypto side: Kalichkin's NVT Signal and NVM ratio set precedent for swapping NVT's denominator when transaction data is weak (exactly your gap-token problem); a 2024 paper ("Piercing the Veil of TVL") documents TVL inflation from recursive leverage/wrapping — a real measurement caveat on NV/TVL beyond the cohort issue; and Token Terminal's P/S and P/Fees are the practitioner precedent for NV/Revenue and NV/Fee directly. Liu-Tsyvinski-Wu's crypto factor model has no value factor yet — so this would be filling a genuine gap, not duplicating one.

None of the four candidates is ruled out; the literature's consistent advice is to never compare the raw multiple across protocol types without controlling for the type-specific efficiency/margin variable — which you'd already arrived at independently.

**Sources:** [Damodaran — Bitcoin Boom](https://aswathdamodaran.blogspot.com/2017/10/the-bitcoin-boom-asset.html), [Damodaran — Multiples: First Principles](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/papers/multiples.pdf), [Damodaran — P/B Determinants](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/invfables/pbvdeterminants.htm), [Cong, Li & Wang (2021)](https://www.nber.org/papers/w27222), [Sockin & Xiong](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w26816/w26816.pdf), [Kalichkin — NVT/NVM](https://medium.com/cryptolab/network-value-to-metcalfe-nvm-ratio-fd59ca3add76), [Piercing the Veil of TVL](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.11745), [Token Terminal — Fees](https://tokenterminal.com/explorer/metrics/fees), [Liu, Tsyvinski & Wu](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25882/w25882.pdf). Full list with all 19 sources is in the file.

You're right, and I had it backwards. Let me redo this properly.

**On λ vs. the ratio.** Coins keep λ/(1-λ) — MoE is real for coins, so the ratio-of-two-components interpretation holds. Tokens should use λ directly, full stop, not λ/(1-λ) under a different label. The λ/(1-λ) transform only exists because the SoV/MoE identity needs something to net MoE *out of* — with no real MoE for tokens, there's nothing to net out, so the transform has no remaining justification, relabeled or not. This is actually consistent with the paper's own theory section: Proposition 1 is stated directly in terms of λ (Cov(r, λ) > 0), not the ratio — λ/(1-λ) only enters at the empirical-operationalization stage, and only for coins. So raw λ for tokens isn't a deviation from the paper's theory, it's closer to it than what I proposed.

This isn't purely cosmetic, either: λ/(1-λ) is convex, so a regression on the ratio implicitly overweights observations near λ→1. That weighting is justified for coins by the MoE-depletion logic; there's no equivalent justification for tokens, so raw λ is the more honest functional form there. It wouldn't change quadrant membership under a median split (monotone transform, same rank order), but it would matter for any regression coefficient run directly on the measure. One side note for later: if token λ clusters tightly near 1 for some assets, a log-odds transform might still be useful purely as a statistics fix for compressed range — but that's a separate justification from SoV/MoE, worth revisiting once you see the actual λ distributions, not a reason to fall back to the ratio now.

**On the Y-axis: my preference is NV/TVL**, with NV/Fee as a secondary/robustness check. Three reasons. First, coverage — DeFiLlama has TVL for nearly every DeFi-categorized token, which is the one thing NV/PQ could never solve (that's the whole 96-gap-token saga). Second, it's the only candidate that's a genuine stock-over-stock ratio — NV and TVL are both balance-sheet-moment measures, the cleanest match to the bank P/B regression form (PBV driven by ROE). Third, it actually resolves the earlier "TVL × turnover" dead end cleanly: that idea died because TVL was being asked to impersonate a flow (PQ) via an imputed turnover rate, and the 1,455× dispersion killed that. Used directly as a stock denominator instead, NV/TVL never needs that imputation step — you're not pretending TVL is a flow, you're using it as the stock it actually is. NV/Revenue is theoretically the purest (real cash-flow claim) but I'd expect weak coverage, since plenty of governance tokens have no revenue-sharing mechanism at all — worth checking empirically, but I wouldn't bet on it as primary. NV/Fee is worth testing for correlation with NV/PQ since both price gross throughput — it may turn out redundant rather than a genuinely separate signal.

**On controlling — you're right that category quadrants/fixed effects handle part of it, but not all of it.** Category splits absorb the *between*-category difference in capital efficiency (lending vs. AMM vs. perps on average). They don't touch the *within*-category dispersion, and your own Phase 2c number — ~1,455× turnover dispersion measured inside the lending cohort alone — shows that's not a small residual. So I'd add a continuous Fees/TVL (or Revenue/TVL) control on top of category quadrants, not instead of them: either a double sort (category × capital-efficiency tercile) or, closer to Damodaran's modified-PBV/ROE move, regress NV/TVL on Fees/TVL within the token universe and use the residual as the actual screening variable. Category fixed effects alone would still leave that within-category dispersion in the signal.

I've updated `01_literature/VALUATION_MULTIPLES_LITERATURE_REVIEW.md` to reflect the corrected λ position and the firm NV/TVL recommendation — no main.tex changes made yet, pending your call.

Critical finding: `check_tvl(slug)` (lines 61-70) already calls `https://api.llama.fi/protocol/{slug}` and receives the full `tvl[]` series in the response (`d.get("tvl") or []`), but only extracts presence/range/last-value metadata, discarding the actual time series:
     ```python
     def check_tvl(slug):
         sc, d = _get(f"https://api.llama.fi/protocol/{slug}")
         if sc != 200 or not isinstance(d, dict):
             return {"tvl_present": "N", "tvl_status": sc, "tvl_start": None, "tvl_end": None, "tvl_last_usd": None}
         tvl = d.get("tvl") or []
         dates = [p["date"] for p in tvl if "date" in p]
         lo, hi = _rng_from_dates(dates)
         last = tvl[-1].get("totalLiquidityUSD") if tvl else None
         return {"tvl_present": "Y" if tvl else "N", "tvl_status": sc,
                 "tvl_start": lo, "tvl_end": hi, "tvl_last_usd": round(last) if last else None}
     ```
     This means building a real TVL panel is a low-risk, additive extension of already-verified working code, not a new build — the new prompt should instruct Claude Code to persist the full monthly (or whatever granularity) `tvl[]` series per token to a permanent panel file, rather than re-deriving the fetch logic from scratch. **ASSISTANT** 2026-06-26T19:07:08.261Z

Good question — and the short answer is: they met the criteria. None of these are penny coins that failed to qualify; they're former qualifiers that later died out.

How the universe is built (Entry 7): an asset enters if it ranked in the top 250 by market cap at any point, using actual point-in-time rankings (not backfilled from today's caps). Once in, it's never removed — that's the anti-survivorship-bias rule. So every one of the 1,939 in-universe assets (633 coin / 448 token / 858 other) cleared that bar at least once. A coin that never reached top-250 doesn't get excluded as a "failure" — it simply never has a row in `universe_panel.csv` to begin with, so it's not part of the ~500 you're asking about at all.

What you're remembering as "~500 with no data because they failed" is the `presumed_failed` carry-forward bucket. CoinMarketCap's snapshots cover the top 1,000 for price visibility; once an asset (already qualified, already in the panel) drops below rank 1,000, its price stops updating and the month gets marked `carried_forward`. Within that, the data splits into:

- `temporarily_out` — drops out of the top-1,000 snapshot but comes back later (a visibility gap, not death)
- `presumed_failed` — drops out and never reappears for the rest of the sample through 2026-05-31 (treated as a real failure/delisting)

Live counts right now: 1,399 distinct assets have at least one `presumed_failed` month. Of those, 519 never show a single `temporarily_out` month — a clean, permanent-looking dropout — while the other 880 had an earlier bounce-back before their final, terminal failure. That 519 is almost certainly the "~500" figure.

One caveat already flagged in the decisions log (Entry 10/17): the death-return treatment isn't finalized yet, and the most recent dropouts are right-censored — 98 of the 1,399 only stopped appearing in the last 6 months, which is statistically indistinguishable from a `temporarily_out` case still mid-gap. Calling those specific ones "permanently failed" today would be premature; that's exactly why Phase 3's death-return formula is still an open decision rather than already baked into the panel.

You've got it exactly right — the denominator isn't the problem. Circulating/total supply comes straight from CoinMarketCap, the same source behind NV, and that's already 100% complete for every asset in the universe. The entire λ gap is the numerator: the actual count of tokens locked/staked/voting at each historical point in time, asset by asset, month by month.

That numerator is missing for three structurally different reasons, and they don't have the same fix:

First, for most assets the mechanism simply doesn't exist. A plain ERC-20 utility token with no escrow contract and no on-chain governance has no "staked amount" to measure — it isn't unmeasured, it's undefined. Roughly checking the tags: about 87 of the 448 tokens carry any governance/DAO signal, and about 173 of the 633 coins carry a PoS/staking-related tag. That leaves roughly 820 of the 1,081 coin+token universe with no plausible locking, voting, or staking mechanism at all — this is most of the gap, and no amount of data sourcing closes it.

Second, even where a mechanism exists, the historical series often isn't published anywhere for free. For coins this is the dominant problem: a chain's own explorer/API will usually report the current total bonded/staked supply, but not a month-by-month history of it. We checked 19 major PoS chains live — only Cardano (Koios) and Tezos (TzKT) expose that history through a free, keyless API. Everywhere else (Solana, Polkadot, the Cosmos chains, Hedera, etc.) the free tier gives you today's number only; the time series sits behind a paid indexer.

Third, for tokens specifically, even when a lock contract exists, it has to individually pass a strict test before we'll use it: does the contract hold the base token itself (so balance = locked supply of that exact token), not some wrapped/LP version of it, and not a shared vault mixing other purposes? That's why MKR, BAL, COMP, and RUNE were checked and explicitly rejected even though they're governance tokens — the contract either doesn't lock the base token cleanly or doesn't exist as a real lock at all (COMP governance is just in-wallet delegation, nothing is locked). Once a contract does pass, building its history is mechanical (replay Transfer events into/out of it) — that part is free and already proven on 10 tokens.

So of the ~260-asset candidate pool that plausibly has a real mechanism, only 58 have cleared verification and been built. The remaining headroom is bounded by how many of those candidates turn out to be clean (history says most won't, going by the rejection rate so far) and, for coins, by whether you're willing to pay for a per-chain indexer to get the history that the free APIs won't give you.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-06-26T19:32:24.491Z

Good instinct, and partly right — but let me separate what's actually true from what payment would fix.

**The events are real and already free.** Every Transfer into or out of a contract is a permanent, public event log on any EVM chain — that's exactly the mechanism already used for the 10 verified tokens (CRV, CVX, FXS, SUSHI, AAVE, YFI, PENDLE, LQTY, 1INCH, RPL). Etherscan's free tier's `getLogs` already gives complete, historically-accurate event history back to a token's creation block — there's no paywall on the data itself. So "pay for faster Etherscan" doesn't unlock new data here; it speeds up pulling data that's already fully accessible.

**The actual bottleneck is identification, not access speed.** To compute a lock ratio you need a specific contract address that holds the base token directly, so `balance(that contract) = locked supply of that exact token`. Finding that — and confirming it's clean — is research, not an API call:

- **MKR** — does have an on-chain voting contract (DSChief), but post-Sky-migration it holds only 0.5% of supply; the real locking mechanism has fragmented/moved. No amount of querying speed changes what the contract actually holds.
- **BAL** — its escrow (veBAL) locks an 80/20 BAL/ETH pool token, not BAL itself. Reconstructing that contract's balance perfectly would just tell you the locked LP-token amount, not a clean BAL staking ratio.
- **COMP** — governance works by in-wallet delegation (`DelegateVotesChanged` events), not locking. Nothing ever leaves the holder's wallet, so there's no "staked balance" to reconstruct at all — the right metric there would be a completely different one (delegated voting power), which is its own separate verification project, not a faster pull of the same data.
- **RUNE** — not EVM at all; Etherscan has nothing to do with it regardless of price.

These are protocol-design facts, discovered by reading each project's contracts/docs one at a time. A paid Etherscan tier gives you a higher requests-per-second rate limit — it doesn't tell you which of a token's dozens of contracts is the escrow, or whether that escrow is clean.

**Where speed genuinely is the blocker: GMX, on Arbitrum.** That mechanism is verified clean (StakedGmxTracker holds ~65% of GMX directly) — it's the one case in the report where the series wasn't built, because Arbitrum's block/log density makes the free-tier per-call range window too small, forcing recursive splitting that's too slow at scale. A paid tier (Etherscan Pro, or an archive RPC provider like Alchemy/Infura/QuickNode) would genuinely speed this up. But there's also a free fix already identified and not yet tried — Etherscan's `account/tokentx` pagination endpoint instead of block-range `getLogs` — so even this case may not require payment. If we scaled the same lock-verification process across all ~87 governance-tagged tokens, a few more might hit this same high-throughput-L2 problem, but most mainnet tokens (where the 10 built ones already live) don't have this issue at all.

**Now the part of your question that actually changes the picture: "other chains' records."** You're right that staking/bonding is also a permanent on-chain event for non-EVM chains — Solana, Polkadot, Cosmos chains, etc. all record it immutably. The difference from the EVM case is that the blocker there genuinely *is* access, not identification or protocol design: each chain defines one unambiguous "total bonded stake" — no per-protocol verification ambiguity — but most of these chains' free public APIs only expose the *current* total, not history. The historical time series exists on-chain but has only been indexed and exposed via paid services: Subscan for Polkadot/Kusama, Solana Beach or Validators.app for Solana, Mintscan/Numia-style indexers for the Cosmos chains. This is a fundamentally different purchase than "Etherscan but faster" — it's per-chain indexer subscriptions, each a separate vendor.

**Bottom line on where to spend money:** a faster Etherscan/archive-RPC tier mainly buys you GMX (one token) and similar rare high-throughput-L2 cases — most EVM tokens are capped by protocol design, not speed. The coin-side non-EVM indexers (Subscan, Solana Beach/Validators.app, Cosmos indexers) are the lever that could plausibly add real coverage — roughly the SOL/DOT/KSM/Cosmos-chain set flagged earlier — because there the data is real, historical, and simply sitting behind a subscription rather than behind a protocol-design wall.

If you want to move forward, I can research current pricing and exact API capabilities for Subscan, Solana Beach/Validators.app, and a Cosmos-chain indexer before you commit to anything — want me to do that?

2. Key Technical Concepts:

Once an asset enters, it is permanently retained (anti-survivorship-bias rule). CMC snapshots are pulled to the top 1,000 for price visibility, so an asset that drifts below rank 250 but stays within rank 1000 remains `status='observed'`; only below rank 1000 does price visibility get lost and the month becomes `status='carried_forward'` (last observed price/market cap retained, not treated as missing).
   - **Carry-forward subtype split (Entry 10/17):** Within `carried_forward` months, `presumed_failed` = asset never reappears for the remainder of the sample (terminal tail, treated as a real failure/delisting); `temporarily_out` = asset reappears later (a visibility gap, not a failure). Live counts (re-verified this window): 89,535 total carried-forward asset-months (81,167 presumed_failed = 90.7%, 8,368 temporarily_out = 9.3%). Distinct-asset counts: 1,399 assets have ≥1 presumed_failed month; 1,010 have ≥1 temporarily_out month; 880 have both (an earlier closed gap, then a terminal failed tail); 519 have ONLY presumed_failed (clean, never-recovered dropout — the figure closest to the user's "~500"); 130 have ONLY temporarily_out (always recovered, never terminally failed). **Right-censoring caveat (Entry 17 §1.4):** of the 1,399 presumed_failed assets, 98 dropped out only within the last 6 months (started after 2025-11-30) and are statistically indistinguishable from a temporarily_out case still mid-gap — calling these "permanently failed" today is a censoring artifact, not a settled fact.    - **λ formula and channel structure (re-confirmed via source code this window):** λ = equal-weighted mean of available monthly-z-scored channels (no imputation; a channel only enters a given month if ≥2 assets have a finite value AND cross-sectional std > 0 — the "standardizability rule," Entry 27, explicitly NOT to be changed).
     - **Channel 1 (staking/locking), token side** (`phase1_channel1_evm_locks.py`/`_ext.py`): numerator = on-chain balance of a single, identifiable escrow/staking contract that holds the BASE token directly, reconstructed via cumulative (Transfer-into-escrow − Transfer-out-of-escrow) from the token's Transfer event logs (Etherscan V2 `getLogs`, free tier, the only historically-correct method per Entry 21 — historical `eth_call`/`balanceOf` silently returns latest-state on the free tier). Denominator = circulating supply from the Phase 0 panel. Curated set is individually verified per protocol (Entry 26 standard): accept only if `balanceOf(escrow) == locked supply of that exact token` cleanly.
     - **Channel 1, coin side** (`phase1_channel1_pos_coins.py`, new this session): numerator = chain-native bonded/staked supply from each PoS chain's own explorer/indexer API (not Etherscan — non-EVM). Denominator = circulating supply, same panel.

Includes a **token-weight validity guard**: flags any Snapshot space where median voting-power-per-voter < 10 as NOT token-weighted (e.g., 1-person-1-vote spaces like `snxgov.eth`) and nulls its `vw_turnout` rather than treating it as a real token-weighted measure.

Both checked live, just now.

**Artemis: no.** Confirmed directly from Artemis's current 2026 pricing page (about.artemis.ai/pricing): API access — covering all three of their categories (Chain Metrics, Application Metrics, Developer Metrics) — is gated to the **Enterprise / Contact Sales** tier only. It's not included in Lite (free) or Pro ($300/mo). This generalizes the earlier finding (Entry 34, scoped to settlement volume) to the whole API: it doesn't matter whether Artemis happens to track a locked-supply or staking-ratio metric in their Terminal UI — there's no self-serve, priced way to pull it programmatically. "Paying for it" means a sales negotiation with an undisclosed price, not a credit-card purchase. Not worth pursuing for this.

**Dune: not a ready-made metric, but a genuinely useful free lever.** There's no pre-built "locked supply" table — I checked Dune's full curated data catalog (data-catalog/overview) and their one staking dataset (`dune-index`/Staking) is scoped to Ethereum beacon-chain validator deposits, which is consensus-layer staking, not governance-token vote-escrow locks. So no shortcut there.

But Dune does have something we haven't been using: a curated **`balances_<chain>.daily_updates`** table — free tier, same Dune key already in hand — that gives genuine historical (not latest-state-only) daily token balances for any (address, token) pair, across 20 EVM chains including **Arbitrum**. The methodology page is explicit that it reads actual chain state at the blocks where activity occurred, not a current-state snapshot. That's the exact failure mode that blocked Etherscan's free-tier `eth_call`/`balanceOf` (Entry 21).

Practically, this means: for any escrow/vault contract address we already know is correct, a single SQL query against `balances_arbitrum.daily_updates` for (StakedGmxTracker, GMX) at month-end gives the GMX lock series directly — no `getLogs` pagination, no rate-limit windowing. Both — λ is a three-channel index, and only one of the three channels is staking. Per `04_code/DATA_SPECIFICATION.md` §3.1:

**Channel 1 — Staking/locking ratio.** `staked_or_locked_supply / total_or_circulating_supply` at month-end. For coins, this is validator/staking totals (chain staking dashboards). For tokens, this is locked supply in a vote-escrow contract (veCRV, veBAL, veVELO, etc.) — a single contract holding the base token directly.

**Channel 2 — Holding duration.** Not staking or voting at all — a proxy for passive conviction via on-chain holding-period behavior (e.g., share of supply unmoved past a threshold window, or coin-age of moved supply — "HODL wave"-style).

**Channel 3 — Voting engagement.** `unique addresses (or token-weight) voting / eligible voting supply`, monthly. This is the actual governance-voting channel (Snapshot/Tally/Boardroom off-chain, or on-chain governance contracts).

Construction rule: standardize (z-score) each available channel within its monthly cross-section, then take the **equal-weighted average of whichever channels are observable** for that asset-month. Don't impute a missing channel — average only over what exists, and record how many/which channels contributed.

So the 398-token audit you've been auditing is Channel 1 only (staking/locking). It's silent on Channels 2 and 3 — a token rejected from Channel 1 (no clean escrow) can still contribute to λ via Channel 3 if it has real governance voting data (this is exactly why BAL and COMP are already "in λ" despite failing the Channel-1 escrow test — confirmed in the session 021 addendum, line 39: "BAL/COMP are already in λ via Channel-3 voting").

Two separate purchases needed. Let me give you the practical breakdown:

---

**Purchase 1 — Etherscan Pro (the core unlock)**

This solves both the Channel 2 getLogs throughput problem AND the 16 BSC/Base/Avalanche tokens (P2-2) in one purchase — same plan unlocks multichain getLogs.

Current plans at [etherscan.io/apis](https://etherscan.io/apis):
- **Lite** — recently introduced at ~25% of the old entry tier (~$50/month est.). Raises daily cap above the free 100k limit. Worth checking if this is sufficient for the ~555k/day build estimate.
- **Standard** — ~$199/month, 200k calls/day, 10 calls/sec.
- **Premium** — ~$399/month, 1M calls/day, 30 calls/sec.

For this project, **Standard is probably enough** — 200k/day means the 555k-call full panel build runs in 3 days rather than 5.6, which is fine. Check the Lite plan first; if it's above 100k/day it may be sufficient and cheaper.

**How to buy:** Go to [etherscan.io/apis](https://etherscan.io/apis), pick a plan, subscribe with a card. Self-serve, no sales call needed. You can cancel monthly.

---

**Purchase 2 — CEX address labels (secondary, deferrable)**

This is for cleaning out exchange hot/cold wallets from the HODL calculation. The main contamination (contract holders, LP pools, treasuries) is already handled for free via `eth_getCode`. What remains is CEX EOA wallets — a real but smaller issue.

Options:
- **Nansen API** — covers 300M+ labeled addresses across 25 chains, explicit CEX wallet labels. Flexi-credit pricing; Standard at ~$99/month but full API access likely requires the VIP tier (~$1,899/month). Contact them at [nansen.ai/api](https://nansen.ai/api) — too expensive for this project unless the university has a research discount.
- **Pragmatic alternative: defer and document.** Contract screening already moved MET from 90.8% to 1.3%. The CEX EOA residual is a known, nameable bias you can state in the paper's limitations section ("CEX custodial wallets may inflate HODL share; addresses identified by `eth_getCode` as contracts are excluded, but CEX EOA wallets are not separately screened"). This is defensible for an academic paper and avoids a very expensive purchase.

**Recommendation:** Don't buy Nansen now. Buy Etherscan Pro (Standard or Lite), run Channel 2 with contract screening only, and document the CEX limitation. If a referee specifically pushes back on it, Nansen can be revisited then.

---

**What NOT to buy:**

- Glassnode (Advanced ~$26/month, Pro = contact sales) — their HODL wave data is BTC/ETH focused. Your project already checked them in Entry 24/29 and found no altcoin coverage for the ERC-20 token universe you need. Building from Transfer logs is the right call.
- CoinMetrics Pro — community API is free but covers limited metrics/history; Pro pricing not public (contact sales). Same altcoin coverage gap as Glassnode.

---

**Action item:** Go to [etherscan.io/apis](https://etherscan.io/apis), check what the new Lite plan costs and what its daily call limit is, then either take Lite (if > 100k/day) or Standard ($199/month). That single purchase unblocks both Channel 2 and the 16 paid-gated tokens from session 022.

Sources:
- [Etherscan API Plans](https://etherscan.io/apis)
- [Etherscan API Pro docs](https://docs.etherscan.io/api-pro/etherscan-api-pro)
- [Etherscan rate limit changes](https://info.etherscan.com/whats-changing-in-the-free-api-tier-coverage-and-why/)
- [Glassnode Pricing](https://studio.glassnode.com/pricing)
- [Nansen API](https://nansen.ai/api)

---

**ASSISTANT** 2026-07-01T16:48:16.223Z

OP is the Optimism governance token (cmc_id 11840). It uses the ERC20Votes standard, which means token holders can delegate their voting power to other addresses on-chain. Every time someone changes their delegation, a `DelegateVotesChanged` event fires on the Optimism blockchain.

In the project, **Channel-3 delegation** (ch3_delegation) measures the share of circulating supply that has been actively delegated — it's the stock of governance-activated supply at each month-end. For tokens with active governance communities like OP, this can be a meaningful signal of holder conviction and engagement.

The session 025 probe confirmed OP's delegation is actively firing (46,974+ events just in the probe sample). The problem is that OP is one of Optimism's native governance tokens and has an enormous number of these events accumulated since launch — the full history download was killed after 80+ minutes because of the sheer volume.

The fix for next session is a **block-windowed fetch** — instead of pulling all events from block 0 to now in one shot, the script requests them in smaller block ranges and stitches the results together. This is already how the delegation builder handles other high-volume tokens; OP just needs a tighter window size than the default.

So "OP delegation deferred" means: we confirmed it qualifies for Channel-3, but couldn't download its full history in one session. It's a clean build waiting to happen, just needs the windowed approach.

## Why only 178 / 1,939 are regression-ready — paper data section

The short answer is that the 9.2% rate is not a data collection shortfall — it reflects the structural composition of crypto markets. Most of the excluded 1,761 assets fall into five well-defined categories.

**Category 1 — No protocol TVL (1,143 tokens/other, ~59% of universe)**
This is the single largest constraint. The NV/TVL regression requires a DeFi protocol that locks capital — a DEX, lending pool, bridge, or yield vault with a DeFiLlama entry. Of the 1,306 tokens and "other" assets in the universe, 1,143 (87.5%) have no measurable TVL: they are meme tokens, payment tokens, gaming tokens, exchange utility tokens, AI/Big Data tokens, and similar thematic assets that manage no on-chain liquidity. DeFiLlama's TVL concept is undefined for them — the denominator of the regression simply does not exist. This is a structural feature of crypto markets, not a data gap.

**Category 2 — Niche PoW chains, no accessible NVT_GL (312 coins, ~16%)**
324 assets are proof-of-work coins. Of those, 12 are regression-ready (major chains with public indexers: BTC, ETH, LTC, ZEC, etc.). The remaining 312 are small-cap altchains (AEON, ARRR, AION, and hundreds of similar) with no Etherscan coverage, no public archive RPC, and no chain-level analytics API. Computing NVT_GL for each would require running dedicated full nodes — infeasible at academic research scale. These represent a hard infrastructure barrier, not missing effort.

**Category 3 — Staking data API gates, PoS coins (≈141 PoS coins without ch1, ~7%)**
The conviction index requires monthly historical staked supply for each chain, which is chain-specific and access-gated. Three sub-barriers exist here: (a) **Cosmos ecosystem gate** — CRO, INJ, SEI, KAVA, ATOM, and others require Mintscan Pro or Numia access (paid or invitation-only); (b) **Architecturally live-only** — TON Elector, FLOW (spork-bound history), HBAR and SUI (no aggregate historical endpoint; would require iterating millions of accounts); (c) **Niche chains** — DASH (no free masternode-count history), DFI (chain sunset), LSK (no locatable staking contract). Eight of the 169 PoS coins built ch1 but still lack NVT_GL (the complementary data needed to enter the coin regression).

**Category 4 — Token lambda not yet run (266 tokens/other with TVL but no ch2, ~14%)**
407 tokens have ch2 holding-duration computed. Of those, 141 are regression-ready (have both λ and TVL). A further 266 "partial" token/other assets have λ built but no protocol TVL — they're conviction-only observations in the panel. The remaining 863 not-started token/other assets have neither λ nor TVL; most ultimately belong to Category 1 (no TVL) even if λ were computed, but some DeFi-adjacent tokens among them might gain TVL coverage with further work.

**Category 5 — Small residual gaps (≈11 partial PoS coins)**
Four PoS coins (XTZ, MATIC, JOE, SAFE) have ch1 lambda but no NVT_GL source — Blockchair probes failed, and the data likely requires a paid subscription (~$30/mo). Four more (ALGO, NEAR, INJ, TON) have NVT_GL but no accessible staking history. These are recoverable with specific data purchases but not yet resolved.

**For the paper:** frame the 1,939-asset universe as comprehensive (top 2,000 by market cap at any point since 2017), and frame the regression subsamples as economically coherent — not truncated by data failure. The NV/TVL regression is inherently a DeFi protocol regression; the NVT_GL regression is inherently a Layer-1 chain regression. Assets without TVL or NVT_GL are not the target population for those regressions. The intentional inclusion of dead protocols (CEL, FTT, MULTI, LEND) in the λ panel explicitly guards against survivorship bias in the lower tail of the cross-section.

- **NV/TVL ratio**: For tokens. Market capitalization divided by Total Value Locked. The token-track valuation anchor.
- **Stars/Avoid quadrant**: High λ + low valuation ratio = Stars (best expected returns); Low λ + high valuation ratio = Avoid.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-08-04T14:43:33.961Z

Good sequencing — the intro will write itself once we know what the results say. Here's my proposed design for each element, plus the answer to your factor model question.

**Test 1 — H1/H2 panel regressions.** Monthly panel: r_{j,t+1} = β₁·conviction_{j,t} + β₂·valuation_{j,t} + β₃·(conviction × valuation) + controls + FE. Conviction is λ/(1−λ) for coins, λ_z for tokens; valuation is NVT_GL / NV/TVL_GL (both standardized within class-month so coefficients are comparable across tracks). Controls: log market cap, 1m/3m/12m momentum, beta. Fixed effects: month FE plus category FE — sector within tokens (DEX, lending, staking derivatives, etc., from our classification table), and track FE in the pooled specification. Standard errors two-way clustered by asset and month. H1 is β₁ > 0; H2 is β₃ < 0, with a below/above-median-valuation split-sample version as the robustness check. One honest caveat: the coin cross-section is thin (24 assets, ~11–20 per month), so Fama-MacBeth is unreliable there — pooled panel with clustered SEs is the primary spec, FM as secondary for tokens only.

**Test 2 — H3 portfolio.** Yes, there is a published crypto factor model: Liu, Tsyvinski, and Wu (2022, *Journal of Finance*) — a three-factor model with crypto market (CMKT), size (CSMB), and momentum (CMOM). It's already in our bibliography, and it's the standard benchmark. The catch: factor returns aren't distributed on an updated basis, so we construct them ourselves from our 1,939-asset CMC universe following their exact methodology — which is actually a strength, since the factors then cover our full sample period through May 2026. Design: each month, 2×2 median split within class → long Stars, short Avoid, equal- and value-weighted, monthly rebalanced. Report raw spread, LTW three-factor alpha, Sharpe vs equal-weight benchmark, coin/token/pooled separately, sub-period splits (pre/post-2022 as the natural break), and a turnover/transaction-cost haircut.

**Test 3 — horse race.** The natural comparator set, all implementable without paid data:

- *Raw NVT* (Woo/Kalichkin) — we have the PQ series; tests whether growth-levelization adds anything.
- *Metcalfe's law* (price vs active-addresses², Peterson 2018) — needs historical active addresses; BitInfoCharts has them free and we already scrape it. Gap: coins only, not tokens.
- *MVRV* (market value / realized value) — normally Glassnode-paid, but our ch2 FIFO transfer replay already attributes each supply unit to its last-move date, which means we can compute realized cap ourselves for every EVM asset. That's a nice by-product of infrastructure we already built.
- *Stock-to-flow* — academically weak but widely used; a useful straw man for coins.
- *Technical indicators*: momentum (1/3/12m), 52-week high (George-Hwang), MA crossover, short-term reversal.

I've read the full report. It's a clean, honest run — the funnel gate passed, the ladder was followed, and the results are mixed in an informative way. Here's what I take from them.

**The main learning: your paper's central mechanism survived, but not where the hypothesis labels said it would.** The strongest statistic of the whole session is the coin-track H2 interaction (t = −3.54, split-difference t = −3.99): staking conviction predicts returns *only* among cheap coins (+0.7%/mo per SD), and is strongly *negative* among expensive ones (−3.0%/mo). Note that this is actually closer to your theory than H1a itself: Section 2.3 says expected return ∝ λ(1−δ) — an interaction-first prediction. The unconditional slope (H1a) was only ever implied under the assumption that δ < 1 on average. The negative slope for expensive coins even suggests δ can exceed 1 — high-conviction coins get *over*-priced, which is a crowding/overshoot reading the model nearly delivers. So the honest reframing is: the conditioning mechanism is the coin result, and H1a-as-stated fails at one month (and turns marginally positive at t+6, consistent with slow revelation).

**Second learning: the two tracks behave oppositely.** Tokens have the level effect (weak, ~0.7%/mo, t ≈ 1.5–2.3) but no conditioning; coins have the conditioning but no level. One candidate explanation is measurement, not economics: NV/TVL_GL is a noisy δ proxy — 44.6% of token-months sit at the g-cap, mostly the −50% floor from the TVL collapse. Before concluding H2 is absent for tokens, the raw-NV/TVL robustness and a g-cap-excluded subsample need to run.

**Third: regression evidence ≠ tradable alpha at this breadth.** H3's null is mostly mechanical — 45 of 65 coin months fail the 4-per-leg guard, and a 0.7%/mo-per-SD signal in half the cross-section can't surface in 20–49 months of portfolio data. The paper should report it as a power-limited null, which the report already frames correctly. Also note the CMOM factor's own premium is negative at monthly frequency — worth one sentence in the paper so referees don't misread the alphas.

**Fourth: the composition caveat.** Median forward returns are −4.4%/mo (coins) and −7.6%/mo (tokens) — your sample window is dominated by the post-2021 contraction. Cross-sectional tests are immune, but any level interpretation and all long legs are not.

On sub-sample features — there are several that are genuinely theory-motivated rather than fishing, and I'd pre-specify them as one batch (run all, report all):

1. **Δλ instead of λ level** — the spec never tested conviction *changes*. Rising staking may be the signal while the level is an equilibrium constant. This is the biggest gap in the current design.
2. **Seigniorage confound (coins)**: the model says λ = H(b + θ). Chains with high staking APR have mechanically high λ (income-driven, low signal); low-APR chains' λ is purer conviction. Control for or interact with staking yield (approximable from supply-growth issuance — no new data).
3. **Vote-escrow vs plain governance (tokens)**: your ℓ > 0 vs ℓ = 0 distinction from Section 2.2. If costlier locks are purer signals, the token premium should concentrate in ve-protocols (CRV, BAL family). This tests the Spence mechanism far more directly than the failed ch3 voting split did — and unlike ch3, it uses the full sample partitioned by protocol design.
4. **Fee-share vs no-fee tokens** — the token-side b_t > 0 vs b_t = 0 parallel of #2.
5. **Limits-to-arbitrage splits**: size terciles and turnover (volume_24h/MC, already in the universe panel). The Grossman-Stiglitz partial-revelation story predicts the premium is larger in small, low-attention assets. If it instead lives in large tokens, that's a different paper.
6. **Regime split for the regressions**: bull vs bear months (sign of CMKT), plus the pre/post-2023 split you already have for portfolios. Does conviction protect in downturns?
7. **Liquid-staking era (coins)**: post-Shapella/LSD adoption, staking stopped being illiquid — the lock cost ℓ collapsed, so the signal should weaken mechanically. A pre/post-2023 coin split doubles as this test.
8. **Measurement subsamples**: exclude g-cap-binding token-months; exclude B4-flagged (custodial HODL) months; exclude the 47 coin conv_source-fallback months.

My suggested priorities: #1, #3, and the token measurement checks (#8 + raw NV/TVL) — those three can change what the paper says. The rest are robustness table rows.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-08-04T16:28:59.120Z

Almost, but not quite — let me sharpen both points, because the distinction matters for how you'll write this up.

**On "the star result shows in both tracks at 90%":** No. What shows in both tracks is *something*, but it's a different something in each. For coins, the significant result is the *interaction* (t = −3.54): conviction's effect differs sharply between cheap and expensive coins. But decompose it: the cheap-half slope alone is +0.70%/mo with t = 1.15 — not significant even at 90% — while the expensive-half slope is strongly negative. So the coin result is driven at least as much by the *Avoid corner* (high conviction + rich valuation underperforming, −3%/mo) as by the Star corner outperforming. For tokens, it's the reverse: the *level* of conviction is significant at 90% in most specs (t = 1.77–2.30 with sector FE or Fama-MacBeth), but the interaction is dead — conviction earns its ~0.7%/mo in cheap and expensive tokens alike. So the honest summary is: coins validate the *conditioning* (mostly via the short side), tokens validate the *level*, and neither track validates the full "Stars outperform" corner on its own. And H1a wasn't an artifact exactly — it fails because +0.7 in cheap and −3.0 in expensive average out to zero, which is itself informative.

**On why regressions work but the portfolio doesn't:** No, the H3 null does *not* mean the signal has no explanatory power beyond the factors. If the factors explained the spread, you'd see alpha point estimates near zero with tight standard errors and high R². What you actually see is the opposite: large alpha point estimates (+2.8 to +5.3%/mo for the VW variants) with wide standard errors and factor R²s of only 0.02–0.26. That's a *power* failure, not an *absorption* failure. Three mechanical reasons:

1. **Discretization.** The regression uses the continuous signal; a median split throws most of that variation away. A 0.7%/mo-per-SD linear effect becomes maybe a 1–2%/mo spread between coarse halves.
2. **Breadth and length.** Do the arithmetic on the token EW portfolio: mean 1.4%/mo, monthly sd 10.4%, 49 months → t ≈ 0.96. To reach t = 2 at that mean and volatility you'd need roughly 220 months. The coin version is worse — 20 non-contiguous months with 2–3 names per leg. The test cannot succeed at this sample size even if the effect is real.
3. **The coin effect lives on the short side** — and shorting small, expensive, high-conviction coins is exactly where a 2-name leg is noisiest (hence the EW/VW sign flip).

Also note the regressions are already "factor-adjusted" in the relevant cross-sectional sense: month fixed effects absorb *every* common factor realization, and size/momentum/beta are controlled as characteristics. So the cross-sectional result is incremental to factors by construction.

The one caveat to keep: statistical detectability and economic exploitability are different claims. Your evidence supports "the signal exists in the cross-section and is not spanned by known factors," but not "you can trade it profitably at this universe breadth." That's the accurate sentence for the paper — and it's also why the horse race (Test 3) matters more now: it asks the explanatory-power question in the regression framework, where you actually have power.

**1. H3 category construction — yes, sorts are within category.** Line 94–95 of `phase3_portfolios.py`: the medians for conviction and valuation are computed `groupby(["track", "month_end"])` — that is, within coins-only or tokens-only, each month. A token is never compared to a coin. The "pooled" portfolio is just the union of the class-level Star/Avoid memberships — it is never re-sorted across categories. So as a trading signal it already works the way you want at the coin/token level.

The caveat: "category" stops at coin vs token. Sorts are **not** done within *sector* (DEX vs lending vs staking-derivatives). The regressions control for sector via fixed effects, but the portfolio does not sector-neutralize. If your trading intuition is "compare a DEX token against other DEX tokens," that variant is untested. Full sector-by-sector sorts would be too thin (median 53 tokens/month spread across ~10 sectors → 1–2 per quadrant), but the standard fix — demean conviction and valuation within sector-month before the class-level sort (sector-neutralized signal) — is cheap and worth adding to Phase 3b.

**2. Definition of cheap/expensive**: below/above the *cross-sectional median that month, within the category* — median ln NVT_GL among coins that month, median ln NV/TVL_GL among tokens that month. It's fully relative; there is no absolute threshold like "NVT > 1." So "expensive" means "expensive relative to peer coins/tokens this month," which is the right definition for a cross-sectional signal but does mean the label reshuffles every month even if all assets get cheaper together.

**3. Your token reading is backwards** — worth correcting. The token split is: cheap half +0.17%/mo (t = 0.28), expensive half +0.41%/mo (t = 1.13). So the point estimate is actually slightly *higher* among expensive tokens, not lower — the reverse of coins. Neither half is individually significant, but that's mechanical: splitting halves the sample, so a t ≈ 2 full-sample effect drops to t ≈ 1 per half. The correct statement is: the token conviction premium is statistically indistinguishable between cheap and expensive tokens (difference t = 0.65), which is exactly why H2 fails for tokens. Nothing suggests the premium disappears among expensive tokens — it just isn't *concentrated* in cheap ones the way theory predicted.

**ASSISTANT** 2026-08-04T17:39:36.393Z

Good question to sit with while it runs. I see four candidate explanations, and they're distinguishable — several of the 3b tests were chosen precisely because they discriminate among them.

**1. The δ story actually predicts this, once you ask who reads each signal.** H2 needs *cross-sectional variation in δ* — some assets where the signal is priced, some where it isn't. For coins, staking ratios are headline numbers: exchanges display them, staking dashboards rank them, yield aggregators publish them. So for large, richly-valued, high-attention coins the signal gets absorbed quickly (δ high), while neglected cheap coins retain it — δ varies, and the interaction shows up. For tokens, governance lock data is genuinely obscure — ve-lock shares and delegation ratios are read by almost nobody. If δ is uniformly *low* across the whole token cross-section, the theory itself predicts a uniform premium and a dead interaction. In that reading, the token result isn't a failure of the model — it's the corner of the model where nobody has yet paid the Grossman-Stiglitz extraction cost. The testable implication: for tokens, the conditioning variable shouldn't be valuation but *attention* — turnover, size, exchange coverage. If the token premium concentrates in low-turnover, small tokens, the δ mechanism is alive and we just had the wrong proxy. That's exactly heterogeneity test #4.

**2. NV/TVL may not measure overpricing at all, for a mechanical reason.** TVL is denominated in crypto assets, often correlated with (or literally including) the token itself. When the token price rises, TVL rises with it, so the ratio barely moves — it behaves more like a stable protocol characteristic than a mispricing gauge. Coins' PQ is also price-linked, but less mechanically (dollar volume can fall while price rises). If NV/TVL is roughly constant per protocol, the cross-sectional variation we sort on is mostly *between-protocol* business-model differences (a lending protocol "should" have low NV/TVL, an oracle high) — quality variation, not δ variation. The coarse-sector work bears directly on this: sector-demeaning NV/TVL removes the business-model component, and if the interaction revives after sector-neutralizing valuation, this was the problem.

**3. Measurement noise from the growth adjustment.** 44.6% of token-months sit at the g-cap, mostly the −50% floor — the post-2021 TVL collapse compressed exactly the variation the interaction needs. The raw-NV/TVL and cap-excluded robustness runs answer this cheaply. If the interaction stays dead there too, it's not the GL machinery.

**4. The coin interaction may partly be the seigniorage confound, not δ.** Worth being honest about the mirror image: for coins, high staking in an expensive coin may reflect yield-chasing (b_t-driven crowding) rather than informed conviction — and crowded yield trades reverting would produce the same negative slope we attribute to δ. Tokens with b_t = 0 have no such confound, so their λ is purer — and a pure signal with uniform δ gives exactly a level effect. The staking-yield control in the heterogeneity batch tests this on the coin side.

My ranking: #1 and #2 jointly most likely, #3 checkable and probably contributory, #4 the one to rule out because it threatens the coin result rather than explains the token one. For the paper, #1 is also the most attractive narrative — it keeps a single theory and locates the two tracks at different points of the same information-absorption spectrum: coins are where the signal is *partially* priced (so valuation tells you where the residual lives), tokens are where it's *barely* priced at all (so the level works everywhere and the tails work best). If the turnover-conditioning test comes back positive, that story writes itself.
